(مكية [إلا الآيات 26 و 32 و 33 و 57، ومن آية 73 إلى غاية آية 80 فمدنية] وآياتها 111 [نزلت بعد القصص]) بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمنِ الرَّحِيمِ

*Subhana* (سُبْحانَ) is a proper name for glorification (*tasbih*), like *Uthman* for a man. Its accusative case is governed by a hidden verb whose expression is omitted. Its implied sense is: "I glorify Allah, *subhana*." Then *subhana* takes the place of the verb and serves in its stead, indicating a thorough declaration of God's transcendence above all the ugly attributes that the enemies of Allah ascribe to Him [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "the ugly attributes that the enemies of Allah ascribe to Him" mean the People of the Sunnah (Ahl al-Sunnah), who hold that He, exalted is He, is the creator of all events, including the actions of servants and other things, good or evil. This is in contrast to the Mu'tazilah, who claim that the servant creates his own act, so that it is within his power and he can be legitimately obligated to perform it. The People of the Sunnah rely on such verses as "Allah is the Creator of all things" (Qur'an 39:62) and "Allah created you and what you do" (Qur'an 37:96). This does not negate the servants' free choice in their actions, since they affirm for them *kasb* (acquisition) in those actions, as established in the science of monotheism (*'ilm al-tawhid*). (ʿ)]]. *Asra* (أَسْرى) and *sara* (سرى) are two dialectal forms. *Laylan* (لَيْلًا) is in the accusative as an adverb of time.

If you say: "Night journey (*isra'*) happens only at night, so what is the purpose of mentioning the night?" [[Mahmud said: "If you say: night journey happens only at night, so what is the purpose of mentioning the night...?" Ahmad said: The night has been paired with the night journey in a context where this answer does not fit, as in His words, "Travel by night with your family in a part of the night" (Qur'an 11:81), and His words, "Travel by night with My servants" (Qur'an 44:23). The apparent meaning, and Allah knows best, is that the purpose of mentioning the night, although the night journey already implies it, is to make the motion vivid in the listener's mind. Since the night journey indicates two things, namely the movement and that it happens at night, one of the two is singled out for mention to strengthen it in the addressee's mind and to draw attention to it as the intended point. A parallel is found in singling out one of the meanings of a previously mentioned word that is combined with something else, such as His words, "Allah said: Do not take two gods; He is only one God" (Qur'an 16:51). The word for two (*ithnayn*) indicates duality and the class of gods, and similarly the singular indicates unity. The point is to draw attention because duality is the intended meaning. Likewise, the wording is meant to awaken the hearer, because unity is what is intended in "He is only one God." Had he said only "He is a god," it would have given the impression that the important matter is affirming divinity for Him, whereas the purpose of the speech is only to affirm His unity, and Allah knows best.]] I say: by using the indefinite *laylan* he meant to reduce the duration of the night journey, that it took place in part of the night, from Mecca to Syria, a journey of forty nights. The indefiniteness here indicates the meaning of "a part." This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Hudhayfah: *min al-layl*, "of the night," meaning part of the night, as in His words, "And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act" (Qur'an 17:79), that is, the command to stand in prayer during part of the night.

Scholars differed about the place from which he was taken by night. It is said that it was the Sacred Mosque (al-Masjid al-Haram) itself, and this is the apparent view.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "While I was in the Sacred Mosque, in the Hijr beside the House, between sleeping and waking, Gabriel (peace be upon him) came to me with the Buraq" [[Agreed upon (by al-Bukhari and Muslim), from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah, in a lengthy form.]]. It is also said that he was taken from the house of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, and that by "the Sacred Mosque" is meant the sacred precinct (*al-haram*), because it surrounds the mosque and is connected with it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The whole sacred precinct is a mosque." It is also reported that he was sleeping in the house of Umm Hani after the night prayer, and was taken by night, then returned in the same night and recounted the story to Umm Hani. He said: "The prophets were shown to me, and I prayed with them." He rose to go out to the mosque, and Umm Hani caught hold of his garment. He said, "What is the matter?" She said, "I fear that your people will call you a liar if you tell them." He said, "Even if they call me a liar." He went out and Abu Jahl sat down with him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told him about the story of the night journey. Abu Jahl said:

"O assembly of the Banu Ka'b ibn Lu'ayy, come and tell them!" Some clapped their hands, and some put their hands on their heads in wonder and denial.

Some who had believed in him apostatized. Some men went to Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "If he said this, he has spoken the truth." They said: "Do you affirm him in that?" He said: "I affirm him even regarding what is more distant than that." Therefore he was named *al-Siddiq* (the Truthful).

Among them were some who had travelled to Syria. They asked him to describe the mosque, so Jerusalem was displayed to him, and he began looking at it and describing it to them. They said: "As for the description, he has got it right." They said: "Tell us about our caravan." He told them the number of its camels and their conditions, and said: "It will arrive on such-and-such a day at sunrise, led by a grey camel." So they went out running that day toward the pass. One of them said: "By Allah, this is the sun, it has risen!" Another said: "By Allah, this is the caravan, and it has come, led by a grey camel as Muhammad said." Yet they did not believe, and said: "This is nothing but manifest magic."

He was also taken up to heaven that same night. The ascent began from Jerusalem. He informed the Quraysh also of what he had seen of the marvels in heaven, that he met the prophets, reached the Frequented House (*al-Bayt al-Ma'mur*) and the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary (*Sidrat al-Muntaha*).

They differed about the time of the night journey. It is said it was one year before the Hijrah. It is related from Anas and al-Hasan that it was before the Prophethood (*al-ba'th*). They also differed about whether it happened while awake or in a dream. It is related from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "By Allah, the body of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was not missing, but he was taken up in spirit" [[Ibn Ishaq said in the *Maghazi*: "Some of the family of Abu Bakr narrated to me from 'A'ishah this (report), but with 'was taken by night' in place of 'was taken up.'" Ibn Ishaq said: "Ya'qub ibn 'Utbah narrated to me from Ibn Mu'awiyah, who said: It was a true vision from Allah."]]. It is related from Mu'awiyah: "He was only taken up in spirit." It is related from al-Hasan: "It was a dream he saw." Most reports, however, are contrary to this.

"The farthest mosque" (*al-Masjid al-Aqsa*) is Jerusalem, because at that time there was no mosque beyond it. "Whose surroundings We have blessed" means blessings of religion and of the world, because it is the place of worship of the prophets since the time of Moses and the place of descent of revelation, and it is surrounded by flowing rivers and fruitful trees.

Al-Hasan recited *liyurihi* with the letter *ya'* (meaning "that He may show him"). The discourse shifts between the third person and the first person. The reading is: "He took him by night (third person), We blessed (first person), that He may show him (third person, in al-Hasan's reading), of Our signs (first person), that He is (third person)." This shift, known as *iltifat*, is one of the methods of eloquence. "Indeed He is the All-Hearing" of the words of Muhammad, "the All-Seeing" of his deeds, knowing his refinement and sincerity, and therefore He honors him and brings him near in accordance with that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 2–3:

"That you not take" (أَلَّا تَتَّخِذُوا) is read with the yā' (ya), meaning "lest they take" (لئلا يتخذوا), and with the tā' (ta), meaning "i.e., do not take" (أى لا تتخذوا), like your saying: "I wrote to him that he should do such-and-such" (كتبت إليه أن أفعل كذا).

"A Guardian" (وَكِيلًا): one to whom you entrust your affairs.

"The offspring of those whom We carried" (ذُرِّيَّةَ مَنْ حَمَلْنا) is in the accusative by way of specification (نصب على الاختصاص). It has also been said that it is in the vocative (على النداء) for one who reads "do not take" (لا تتخذوا) with the tā' as a prohibition (على النهى). The meaning is: We said to them, "Do not take a guardian besides Me. O offspring of those whom We carried with Noah!"

It may also be that "a guardian" (وَكِيلًا) and "the offspring of those whom We carried" (ذُرِّيَّةَ مَنْ حَمَلْنا) are the two objects of "take" (تتخذوا), meaning: do not make them lords, as in His saying: ﴿nor would he command you to take the angels and the prophets as lords﴾. Among the offspring of those carried with Noah are Jesus and Ezra, peace be upon them.

It is read "offspring of those whom We carried" (ذُرِّيَّةَ مَنْ حَمَلْنا) in the nominative (بالرفع) as a substitute (بدلا) for the wāw of "take" (تَتَّخِذُوا). Zayd ibn Thabit read "dhurriyyah" with a kasra on the dhāl (dhurriyyah). It is narrated from him that he explained it as "the offspring of offspring." God reminded them of the blessing in saving their fathers from drowning: ﴿Indeed, he was a grateful servant﴾. It was said: When he ate, he would say, "Praise be to God who fed me, and had He willed, He would have made me hungry." When he drank, he would say, "Praise be to God who gave me drink, and had He willed, He would have made me thirsty." When he dressed, he would say, "Praise be to God who clothed me, and had He willed, He would have left me naked." When he put on his sandals, he would say, "Praise be to God who shod me, and had He willed, He would have left me barefoot." When he relieved himself, he would say, "Praise be to God who released from me its filth in well-being, and had He willed, He would have held it back." It is also narrated that when he wished to break his fast, he would offer his food to those who believed in him, and if he found one of them in need, he would give it preference over himself.

If you ask: what is the connection of His saying "indeed, he was a grateful servant" to what precedes it? I answer: it is as if it were said: "Do not take besides Me a guardian, and do not associate others with Me, for Noah, peace be upon him, was a grateful servant, and you are the offspring of those who believed in him and were carried with him. So take him as your exemplar, just as your fathers took him as their exemplar."

It may also be that this is the reason for their being singled out and praised, namely that they are the descendants of those carried with Noah; they are thus connected to him, and so they deserve that distinction. It may also be said that this is mentioned upon his mention by way of digression (على سبيل الاستطراد).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 4–6:

﴿And We decreed to the Children of Israel in the Book﴾ and inspired them with a decree that was settled, that is, cut off and definitive: that they would surely corrupt the earth and would surely exalt themselves, that is, behave with arrogance and tyranny. ﴿Surely you will cause corruption﴾ is the answer to an implied oath. It is also permissible that the settled decree takes the place of an oath, so that ﴿surely you will cause corruption﴾ is its answer, as if He had said: "And We swore that you would surely cause corruption." It was also read as "la-tufsadunna" in the passive, and as "la-tafsudanna" with a fatha on the ta, from fasada. ﴿Twice﴾: the first was the killing of Zechariah and the imprisonment of Jeremiah when he warned them of the wrath of God. The second was the killing of John the son of Zechariah and the attempt to kill Jesus the son of Mary. ﴿Servants of Ours﴾, and it was read as "ʿubaydan lana." What is most commonly said is "ʿibad Allah" (servants of God) and "ʿabid al-nas" (slaves of people). They were Sennacherib and his armies [[The saying "Sennacherib and his armies" refers to the king of Babylon, and Nebuchadnezzar was the son of his son, and was one of his scribes. The same is in al-Khazin. (ʿA)]]. It was also said that they were Nebuchadnezzar. From Ibn ʿAbbas: Goliath. They killed their scholars, burned the Torah, destroyed the Temple, and took seventy thousand of them captive.

If you ask: How was it permissible for God to send the disbelievers against them in this way and empower them over them? [[The question "How was it permissible for God to send the disbelievers against them in this way" is based on the premise that He, exalted is He, does not do evil and does not will it, which is the position of the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school). According to the Ahl al-Sunna (the Sunni school), everything that occurs is His act and His will, even if it is evil, so there is no question. (ʿA)]] I say: The meaning is that We left them to what they did and did not prevent them, and that God, mighty and exalted, attributed the sending of the disbelievers against them to Himself. It is like His saying: ﴿And thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others, because of what they earned﴾ [6:129], and like the saying of the one who supplicates. He varied their expressions. He attributed the ravaging (al-jaws, which is wandering through the homes with corruption) to them. So the destruction of the Temple and the burning of the Torah are among the ravaging attributed to them. Talha read "fa-ḥāsū" with a ḥāʾ. It was also read "fa-jawwasū." And "khilāl al-diyār" (through the homes).

If you ask: What is the meaning of ﴿the promise of the first of them﴾? I say: The meaning is the promise of punishment for the first of them, and ﴿it was a promise to be fulfilled﴾. That is, the promise of punishment was a promise that must be carried out.

Then ﴿We gave you back the turn﴾, that is, the state and the victory over those who were sent against you, when you repented and returned from corruption and arrogance. It was said: it is the killing of Nebuchadnezzar and the rescue of the Children of Israel from their captives and their wealth, and the return of the kingdom to them. And it was said: it is David's killing of Goliath. ﴿And We made you more numerous in manpower than you were﴾.

The nafīr (the band of men who go forth with a man from his people). It was also said: it is the plural of nafr, like ʿabīd and maʿīz.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 7:

Ay (i.e., ṭ) al-iḥsān wa-l-isāʾa (goodness and evil): both pertain only to yourselves; the benefit and harm do not extend to others. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I have neither done good to anyone nor done evil to anyone," and he recited: ﴿So when the promise of the second time comes, We will send against you [others] to distress your faces﴾ [[Qawluhu: fa-idhā jāʾa waʿdu al-marrati al-ākhira baʿathnāhum: that is, Our servants, who in this second time are the Persians and the Romans. Allah sent against them a king of the kings of Babylon called Khurush. He entered Syria with armies, killed and took captives, until he nearly annihilated the Children of Israel, but remnants of them survived and multiplied, and they held leadership in Bayt al-Maqdis until they altered and introduced innovations, so Allah empowered against them Titus son of Vespasian the Roman, who ruined their lands and expelled them from them. Bayt al-Maqdis remained in ruin until the caliphate of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, and then the Muslims rebuilt it by his command. Ends from al-Khazin. (ʿ)]] — to distress your faces: this is elided because its mention earlier indicates it. The meaning of li-yasūʾū wujūhakum is: that they may make the marks of distress and dejection visible on them, like His saying: ﴿the faces of those who disbelieved will be darkened﴾. It is also read as liyasūʾa, with the pronoun referring to Allah, or to the promise, or to the raising up. And lanasūʾa with the nūn. In ʿAlī's reading: lanasūʾanna and liyasūʾanna, and it is read as lanasūʾan with the light nūn. The lām in li-yadkhulū, according to this, is connected to an elided element, which is: and We raised them up so that they might enter. The lanasūʾa is the answer to idhā jāʾa. Mā ʿalaw is the object of yutabbirū, meaning: that they might destroy everything they overpowered and seized. Or it means: the duration of their dominance.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 8:

"It may be that your Lord will have mercy upon you [after the second time]. But if you return [to sin] [a third time], We will return [to punishment]." And they did return, so God restored the retribution upon them by empowering the Kasras (Persian kings) and imposing tribute upon them. And from al-Hasan: "They returned, so God sent Muhammad, and they give the jizya (poll tax) willingly while they are humbled." And from Qatadah: "Finally, the last of that was that God sent against them this tribe of the Arabs, and they will be in torment at their hands until the Day of Resurrection." ﴿Ḥaṣīran﴾ means a prison, a confinement. It is said that the prison is called maḥṣar and ḥaṣīr. And from al-Hasan: "a spread-out [carpet], as a woven mat (ḥaṣīr) is spread out."

[[His saying "as a woven mat is spread out" means: al-marmūl, i.e. woven, as stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]]

"For that which is most upright." That is: for the state that is the most upright and firmest of states. Or: for the religion (milla). Or: for the way (tariqa). And wherever you take it, you will not find with affirmation the refined eloquence that you find with omission, because in leaving out the described thing there is a grandeur (fakhama) that is lost when it is made explicit.

[Recited] "wa-yubashshir" with the lightened (takhfif) form.

If you ask: how did he mention the righteous believers and the disbelievers, and not mention the sinners (fasiqa)? I answer: people at that time were either a pious believer or a polytheist, and the rank of those in an intermediate position (ashab al-manzila) only came about afterwards [[His saying "and the rank of those in an intermediate position only came about afterwards" means the sinners. The affirmation of an intermediate position (al-wasita) is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila, not of the People of the Sunna, for in their view sin does not remove faith. (Ā)]] between the two ranks.

If you ask: what is "and that those who do not believe" (wa-anna alladhina la yu'minun) coordinated with? I answer: it is coordinated with "that for them is a great reward" (anna lahum ajran kabiran), in the sense that he gives good news to the believers with two kinds of good news: of their reward, and of the punishment of their enemies. It is also permissible that it means: and he informs that those who do not believe are punished.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 11:

It means: a person calls upon Allah in anger for evil against himself, his family, and his property, just as he calls upon Him for good. This is like His saying, ﴿Had Allah hastened for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good﴾. And ﴿man has always been hasty﴾, rushing to seek everything that falls into his heart and occurs to his mind, not deliberating over it with the deliberation of one who reflects.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he handed a captive over to Sawdah bint Zam'ah, and the captive began moaning at night. She said to him, "What is wrong with you that you moan?" He complained of the pain of the *qidd* (a strip of untanned rawhide cut from a hide; in al-Sihah, *qidd* is defined as a thong cut from untanned hide). So she loosened his bonds. When she slept, he drew out his hand and fled. When the Prophet (ﷺ) rose in the morning, he summoned her and was informed of the matter. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said, "O Allah, cut off her hands." Sawdah raised her hands, expecting a response and that Allah would cut off her hands. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I asked Allah to make my curse and my supplication fall upon those among my family who do not deserve mercy, because I am a human being who becomes angry as human beings become angry. So let Sawdah return her hands."

[I have not found it from this route. Al-Waqidi narrated it in his Maghazi from the narration of Dhakwan from Aisha, that the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon her with a captive and said to her, "Keep watch over him." She said, "I became occupied with a woman, and he went out, and I did not notice." Then he came in asking about him, and I said, "By Allah, I do not know." He said, "May Allah cut off your hand," and he mentioned something similar to what preceded. We also narrated it in the ninth part of the hadith of al-Mukhlis, takhrij of al-Baqqal. He said: Ibn Abi Dawud narrated to us, Ahmad ibn Salih narrated to us, Ibn Abi Fudayk narrated to us from Ibn Abi Dhi'b from Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Ata from Dhakwan with this.]

It is permissible that by "the human being" is meant the disbeliever, and that he calls for punishment mockingly and hastens it, just as he calls for good when hardship touches him. And ﴿man has always been hasty﴾: meaning that the punishment will certainly come to him, so what is this haste? It is narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: It is al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who said: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You," [the verse], and he was granted his request, and his neck was struck, put to death *sabran* (bound and killed in cold blood).

There are two interpretations. The first is that the night and the day are themselves two signs, so the annexation (idafa, the construct relation) in "the sign of the night" and "the sign of the day" is explanatory, like the annexation of a number to what is counted. The meaning would be: We obliterated the sign which is the night, and made the sign which is the day illuminating (mubsira).

The second is that the intended meaning is: And We made the night and the day two signs, meaning the sun and the moon. So "We obliterated the sign of the night" means: We made the night obliterated in its light, effaced and dark, so that nothing in it can be discerned, just as nothing can be discerned in an erased tablet. "And We made the day illuminating" means that things are seen and made clear in it. Or it means: "We obliterated the sign of the night," which is the moon, in that We did not create for it a ray like the ray of the sun, by which things are seen clearly; and We made the sun a source of rays, by whose light everything is seen. ﴿That you may seek bounty from your Lord﴾, meaning that you may, by the whiteness of the day, reach the clarity of your deeds and manage your livelihoods. ﴿And that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾, meaning, through the alternation of the two new things, and what you need of it. Were it not for this, no one would know the calculation of times, and affairs would be disrupted. ﴿And everything﴾ which you need in your religion and your worldly life ﴿We have detailed﴾, meaning We have made it clear with a clarity that admits no confusion, removing your excuses, and We have not left you any proof against Us.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 13–14:

*Ṭāʾirahu* (his bird): his deeds. We have already verified the discussion of this in Surah al-Naml. Ibn ʿUyayna said: it derives from your saying *ṭāra lahu sahm* (an arrow flew for him), meaning when it came out. The sense is: We have made binding upon him what flew out of his deeds. The meaning is that his deeds cling to him as inseparably as a necklace or a shackle, which cannot be removed from him. From this is the Arabic proverb: *taqalladahā ṭawqa al-ḥamāma* (he wore it like the collar of the dove). Their saying: *al-mawt fī al-riqāb* (death is in the necks), and *hādhā rabqatun fī raqabatihi* (this is a noose around his neck). On the authority of al-Ḥasan: "O son of Adam, a scroll has been spread out for you; when you are resurrected, it will be hung around your neck."

It is also recited *fī ʿunqihi* with the *nūn* pronounced with sukūn. It is recited *nukhriju* with the *nūn*, and *yukhriju* with the *yāʾ*, the pronoun referring to God, Exalted is He.

*Yukhraju* is recited in the passive voice, and *yakhruju* (it comes out) with the subject referring to the bird. That is, the bird brings forth a book, and *kitāban* is in the accusative as a *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative). It is also recited *yalqāhu* with the *shadda* in the passive voice. *Yalqāhu manshūran* are two descriptions of the book; or *yalqāhu* is a description and *manshūran* is a *ḥāl* of *yalqāhu*. *Iqra'* (Read!) is said as an implied speech. On the authority of Qatadah: on that day, whoever was not a reader in the world will read.

*Bi-nafsika* is the agent of *kafā* (suffices). *Ḥasīban* is a *tamyīz* (specification), and it has the meaning of *ḥāsib* (reckoner), like *ḍarīb al-qidāḥ* (the one who strikes the arrows) meaning *ḍāribuhā*, and *ṣarīm* meaning *ṣārim*; Sibawayh mentioned both. *ʿAlayka* is connected to it, from your saying *ḥasiba ʿalayhi kadhā* (it was reckoned against him such-and-such).

It may also mean "sufficient," placed in the position of "witness," so it takes *ʿalā*, because the witness suffices the claimant in what concerns him. If you ask: why is *ḥasīban* mentioned in the masculine? I say: because it stands in the position of witness, judge and governor, since these matters are usually undertaken by men; so it is as if it were said: "Your soul suffices you as a man reckoner." It is also permissible to interpret *nafs* (soul) as *shakhṣ* (person), as one says *thalāthatu anfus* (three persons).

Al-Ḥasan, whenever he recited it, would say: "O son of Adam, by God, He has been just to you when He made you the reckoner of your own soul."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 15:

Meaning: every soul bearing a burden bears only its own burden, not the burden of another soul. ﴿And We would never punish﴾ — and it is not fitting for Us, in a manner that wisdom calls for, that We punish [[a people until We have sent a messenger to them, so that the proof becomes binding upon them. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Its meaning is: it is not fitting for Us, in a manner that wisdom calls for, that We punish a people until the proof is established against them by the sending of a Messenger..." etc.]] a people until We have sent a messenger, so that the proof is binding upon them.

Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This objection is directed also at the Qadariyya, who claim that reason guides to the obligation of reflection and to many of the rulings of God Most High, even if no messenger has been sent; so they are held accountable by their reason, and the deserving of punishment is made consequent upon neglecting to comply with the obligation, since reason, according to them, is sufficient to make knowledge obligatory, indeed to make all the rulings obligatory, on the basis of the principle of rational goodness and badness. As for the Sunni, this objection does not apply to him, for reason, in his view, is a condition for the obligation of the rulings in general, and there is no obligation in his view before the revelation of the sacred laws and the sending of the prophets. At that point the ruling is established and the proof stands, as this verse indicates, the verse which al-Zamakhshari seeks to distort, so it becomes difficult for him and the paths of stratagems are closed before him, because it is the Mighty Book, falsehood does not come to it from before it or behind it. Yes, reason is the foundation for attaining knowledge, not for its obligation, and between attainment and obligation there is a great distance. And God is the Granter of success.

Objection: The proof is binding upon them before the sending of messengers, because with them are the proofs of reason by which God is known, and they neglected reflection while being able to do it, and their deserving of punishment is due to their neglect of reflection on what is with them, and their disbelief for that reason, not due to neglecting the sacred laws, which can only be reached through divine instruction, and acting upon which is not valid before faith. Answer: The sending of messengers is among the means of alerting to reflection and of awakening from the slumber of heedlessness, lest they say: "We were heedless; if only you had sent to us a messenger to alert us to reflection on the proofs of reason."

﴿وَإِذَا أَرَدْنَا﴾

That is, when the time for destroying a people draws near, and little of the period of their respite remains, ﴿We commanded them﴾ [[Al-Zamakhshari's words "We commanded them, so they transgressed" (أمرناهم ففسقوا). In al-Nasafi: "amarna mutrafiha" (أمرنا مترفيها): its affluent ones (mutnamimuha) and its tyrants (jababiratuha). (ع)]] ﴿so they transgressed﴾.

That is, We commanded them to transgress and they did so. The "commanding" is figurative (majaz), because the literal sense of commanding them to transgress would be for Him to say to them, "Transgress!", and this does not occur. It therefore remains that it is figurative. [[Mahmud said: "The literal sense of their being commanded is that He says to them, 'Transgress!' This does not happen, so it remains figurative... etc." Ahmad said: This is a good text, except his statement that they were given bounties in order to give thanks. That is a branch of the principle that God necessarily wills obedience. The truth is that they were given bounties and were commanded to be thankful, but they transgressed and disbelieved, contrary to the command. The command is not the same as the will, according to the principle of the People of Truth (Ahl al-Haqq). And God is the Granter of success.]]

The basis of the figurative usage is that He poured blessings upon them abundantly, and they made these a means to sins and the pursuit of desires. Thus they are as if they were commanded to do so, since the bestowing of blessings caused it. He gave them these blessings only so that they would give thanks, do good with them, and be enabled to perform acts of kindness and piety, just as He created them healthy and strong and empowered them to do good and evil, and asked them to prefer obedience to disobedience. But they preferred transgression. When they transgressed, the word was justified against them, which is the word of punishment, and He destroyed them.

If you say: "Why not claim that its meaning is 'We commanded them to obey, and they transgressed'?" I reply: Omitting what has no indication is not permissible, so how can one omit what is contradicted by the existing evidence? The object of the command is omitted only because "they transgressed" indicates it, and this is a well-known usage.

One says, "I commanded him and he stood up," and "I commanded him and he recited." Nothing is understood from this except that the thing commanded was standing or reciting. If you tried to assume something else, you would be attributing knowledge of the unseen to your interlocutor. This does not conflict with the saying, "I commanded him and he disobeyed me," or "he did not comply with my command," because that contradicts the command and opposes it, and what contradicts a command cannot be the thing commanded. So it would be impossible for the speaker to intend it at all, so that it could be made to indicate the thing commanded. Therefore, in this statement the thing commanded is neither indicated nor intended, since the one who speaks in this way does not intend a thing commanded by his command. It is as if he says, "There was a command from me, but there was no obedience from him," just as one who says, "So-and-so gives and withholds, orders and forbids," is not aiming at a specific object.

If you say: "Would not the established knowledge that God does not command indecency, but commands moderation and good, be evidence that the meaning is 'We commanded them to good, and they transgressed'?" I reply: That is not valid, because His saying "so they transgressed" contradicts it. It is as if you had expressed one thing while claiming to conceal its opposite. Therefore, turning "commanded" to figurative usage is the correct approach.

The parallel of "amara" (commanded) is "shaa" (willed): in both, the object is commonly omitted when what follows indicates it. You say, "If He had willed, He would have shown kindness to you," and "If He had willed, He would have harmed you," meaning: "If He had willed kindness, and if He had willed harm." If you tried to assume the opposite of what you expressed, saying, "The state of the one to whom the will is attributed shows that he is one of the people of kindness or of harm, so I leave the apparent spoken words and assume what the state of the one who wills indicates," you would not be on a sound footing.

Some have interpreted "amarna" (We commanded) as "kathhharna" (We multiplied), and they took "amirtuhu fa-amar" (I commanded him, so he was commanded) to be of the same pattern as "fa'altuhu fa-fa'ala" (I did it to him, so he did it) and "kathharta fa-thabar" (I multiplied it, so it multiplied). In a hadith: "The best property is a sukkah (date-palm row) that is pollinated (ma'burah) and a mare that is fertile (ma'murah)," that is, one that brings much offspring.

It is also narrated that a man among the polytheists said to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), "I see that this matter of yours is insignificant." He (ﷺ) said, "It will increase (sa-ya'mur)." That is, it will multiply and grow greater.

Some readers recited it as ʾāmarnā (from amara, "to command"), and his "amarahu" means that another made him command. Ammarnā means "amarnā" (we commanded), or it is from imāra (rule, governorship), and "amarahu Allāh" means God appointed him.

That is: We made them leaders (umarāʾ) and gave them authority. The kam (how many) is the object of ahlaknā ("We destroyed"). And min al-qurūn ("from the generations") is an explanation (bayān) of kam and its specification (tamyīz), just as a number is specified by its noun, meaning ʿĀd, Thamūd and generations between them, many. By His words, ﴿And sufficient is your Lord as one who is Acquainted and Seeing with the sins of His servants﴾, he draws attention to the fact that sins are the causes of destruction and nothing else, and that He knows them and punishes for them.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 18–19:

من كانت العاجلة همه ولم يرد غيرها كالكفرة وأكثر الفسقة [[Mahmud said: "That is, whoever has the immediate (world) as his concern and desires nothing other than it, like the disbelievers and most of the wicked..." etc. Ahmad said: A similar restriction occurs in the other verse, His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever desires the tillage of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tillage; and whoever desires the tillage of this world, We give him of it, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾. So He introduced "min" (some of) with the tillage of this world, and He made the seeker of the tillage of the Hereafter attain his desire and increased it for him.]] , We bestow upon him from its benefits what We will, upon whomever We wish. So the matter is restricted by two restrictions: one of them is the restriction of the hastened (good) by His will, and the second is the restriction of the hastened (good) for him by his own desire. Such is the situation: you see many of these people wishing for what they wish, yet they are given only a part of it, and many of them wish for that part and are deprived of it, so the poverty of this world and the poverty of the Hereafter gather upon them. As for the believer who is God-fearing, he has chosen his desire, which is the richness of the Hereafter, so he does not care whether he is given a share of this world or is not given it. If he is given in it, well and good; otherwise, poverty may well be better for him and more helpful toward his desire. His saying ﴿for whom We wish﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "lahu," and it is a substitution of part for whole, because the pronoun refers back to "man," which carries the sense of plurality. It was also read as "yashaa'" (He wills). It was said: the pronoun refers to God, the Exalted, so there is no difference in meaning between the two readings. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to the servant, meaning that the servant has what he wills of the world, and that this belongs to one of the common people (al-dahma') whom God wills for it. [[His saying "to one of the common people": in al-Sihah, "dahma' al-nas" means their masses/multitude. (E.)]] It was said: this refers to one who desires the world through the deeds of the Hereafter, like the hypocrite, the show-off, and one who emigrates for worldly gain, and one who fights for booty and fame, as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever's emigration was to God and His Messenger, his emigration is to God and His Messenger; and whoever's emigration was for worldly gain he might obtain or a woman he might marry, his emigration is to that for which he emigrated." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of Umar.]] ﴿Rejected﴾: expelled from the mercy of God. ﴿Their striving﴾: its due portion of striving, and its sufficiency of righteous deeds. Three conditions are stipulated for striving to be thanked: the desire of the Hereafter, by making it the aim of one's concern and withdrawing from the abode of delusion; striving in what one is obligated to do or abstain from; and sound, firm faith. It is reported from some of the early scholars: whoever does not have these three, his deeds will not benefit him: firm faith, sincere intention, and correct action. And he recited this verse. "Thanks of God" means: the reward for obedience.

Kullan (each one), meaning each of the two groups, and the tanwin is a substitute for the genitive noun that was added to it. Numiddu hum: We increase them from Our bounty, and We make the later part of it an extension of the earlier part, not cutting it off, so that We provide for the obedient and the disobedient alike, by way of grace. Wa ma kana 'ata'u Rabbika wa fadlihi mahzuran: that is, not prevented; nothing prevents it from a disobedient person because of his disobedience.

Consider with an eye of reflection how We have made them differ in favour. And in the Hereafter the difference is greater, because it is reward, recompense and bounty, and all of these differ. It is related that some of the nobles and those below them gathered at the door of ʿUmar (raḍiya Allāhu ʿanhu), and permission was given to Bilāl and Ṣuhayb, which grieved Abū Sufyān. Suhayl ibn ʿAmr said: "We were only brought to this by ourselves: they were called and we were called, meaning to Islam; they hastened and we delayed. This is the door of ʿUmar. So how can there be a difference in the Hereafter? And if you envy them over the door of ʿUmar, then what Allah has prepared for them in Paradise is greater." It was also read: "wa-aktharu tafḍīlan" (and greater in preference). It is related from some of them: "O you who boast of your elevation in the assemblies of this world, do you not desire to be exalted in boasting in the assemblies of the Hereafter, which are greater and better?"

From their saying, "he sharpened the blade (shafra) until it sat (qa'adat)," as if it were a spear (ḥarba), meaning it became. The meaning is: you will end up, sitting (fa-taq'uda) as one who has gathered upon himself blame and whatever destruction follows from it, from your God, and abandonment and inability to be helped by the one you made a partner to Him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 23–24:

﴿And your Lord has decreed and commanded, definitively, that you worship none but Him.﴾ Here "an" (أن) is explanatory (mufassira), and "lā ta'budū" (لا تعبدوا) is a prohibition (nahy). Or it means "bi-an lā ta'budū" (بأن لا تعبدوا). ﴿And to parents, good treatment.﴾ That is, "wa-aḥsinū bil-wālidayni iḥsānan" (وأحسنوا بالوالدين إحسانا), or "bi-an tuḥsinū bil-wālidayni iḥsānan" (بأن تحسنوا بالوالدين إحسانا).

It is also read as "wa-awṣā" (وأوصى), and Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) read "wa-waṣṣā" (ووصى). It is related from some of the sons of Mu'adh ibn Jabal: "wa-qaḍā'a rabbika" (وقضاء ربك).

It is not permissible for the preposition "bi" in "bil-wālidayni" to be connected to "al-iḥsān," because the verbal noun (maṣdar) may not precede its complement. The "in" (إن) here is the conditional "in" to which "mā" (ما) has been added for emphasis (ta'kīd), which is why the emphatic nūn has entered the verb. Had "in" stood alone, it would not be correct for the nūn to enter: you do not say "in tukrimanna Zaydan yukrimka," but rather "immā tukrimanhu."

"Aḥaduhumā" (أحدهما) is the subject (fā'il) of "yablughanna," and in the reading "yablughān" it is a substitute (badal) for the alif of the pronoun referring to the two parents. "Kilāhumā" (كلاهما) is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to "aḥaduhumā," both as subject and as substitute. If you ask: had it been said "immā yablughān kilāhumā," "kilāhumā" would be a corroborative (tawkīd) and not a substitute, so why do you claim it is a substitute? The answer: it is conjoined to something that cannot be a corroborative of the dual, so it is included in its ruling and must be like it. If you ask: what harm would it be to make it a corroborative while the thing conjoined to is a substitute, and to conjoin the corroborative to the substitute? The answer: if corroboration of the dual were intended, it would have said only "kilāhumā," but since it said "aḥaduhumā aw kilāhumā," it is known that corroboration is not intended, so it is a substitute like the first.

"Uff" (أفٍّ) is a sound expressing annoyance. It is read in three vowel forms, with and without tanwīn: with kasra, according to its original indeclinable form; with fatḥa, as a lightening of the ḍamma; and with shadda, like "thumma"; and with ḍamma, as following, like "mundhu." If you ask: what is the meaning of "ʿindaka" (عندك)? The answer: it means that they grow old and become helpless, and they are a burden on their child, having no provider but him. They are then in his house and under his care, which is harder for him and requires greater endurance and patience. He may end up performing for them what they used to perform for him in childhood. Thus he is commanded to employ with them gentleness of character, softness of manner, and forbearance, so that he does not say to them, when he is vexed by something loathsome from them or burdensome in their support, "uff," let alone anything more than that. Allah, glory be to Him, has exaggerated in enjoining them, for He began by pairing kindness to them with His own tawḥīd, and joined them in one line with the decree regarding them together, then restricted the matter of respecting them so strictly that He did not permit even the smallest word that escapes the one who is irritated, given the causes and demands of irritation, and given circumstances in which a person's patience can hardly be within his capacity. ﴿And do not scold them﴾: do not rebuke them or reprimand them for what they do that does not please you. "Al-nahy," "al-nahr," and "al-nahm" are siblings (in meaning). ﴿And speak to them a generous word﴾ in place of "uff" and scolding: a gracious, beautiful word, as good manners and conduct befitting nobility require. It was said:

It is that he says: "O my father, O my mother," as Abraham said to his father, "O my father," despite his disbelief. He should not call them by their names, for that is coarseness, bad manners, and the habit of the wicked. [[His words "and bad manners and the habit of the wicked" come from "al-di'ārah," which means immorality, wickedness and corruption, as in al-Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] They said: there is no harm in it when it is not in its proper place, as ʿĀ'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) said: "Abū Bakr granted me such-and-such." [[It is narrated in al-Muwaṭṭa' from al-Zuhrī from ʿĀ'isha, who said: "Abū Bakr had granted me twenty wasqs of date-palms from his property at al-ʿĀliya. When death approached him he said: 'Of all people, none is dearer to me than you.'"]]

It is read as "janāḥ al-dhull" (جناح الذل), and "al-dhull" is read with ḍamma and with kasra. If you ask: what is the meaning of His words "janāḥ al-dhull"? The answer: there are two aspects. The first: the meaning is "and lower for them your wing," as He said, "and lower your wing to the believers," and it is attributed to "al-dhull" or "al-dhill," as Ḥātim is attributed to "al-jūd" (generosity), meaning: lower for them your humbled or tamed wing. The second: you make for their humility, or their humbling, a lowered wing, as Labīd made the north wind a hand and strength a bridle, for the sake of exaggeration in humility and modesty toward them. ﴿From mercy﴾: from the excess of your mercy toward them and your tenderness toward them, because of their old age and their need today for one who was, yesterday, the neediest of God's creatures toward them. Do not be content with your mercy toward them, which has no permanence, but pray to Allah that He have mercy on them with His lasting mercy, and make that a recompense for their mercy upon you in your childhood and their raising you. If you ask: pleading for mercy on their behalf is valid only if they are Muslims. The answer: if they are disbelievers, he may still ask for mercy on their behalf on condition of faith, and may pray to Allah for their guidance and direction. Some people said: prayer for disbelievers was permitted and then abrogated. Ibn ʿUyayna was asked about giving charity on behalf of the dead, and he said: all of that reaches him, and nothing is more beneficial to him than seeking forgiveness. If there were anything better than it, He would have commanded you to do it for the two parents. Allah, glory be to Him, repeated in His Book the injunction concerning parents. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "The pleasure of Allah is in the pleasure of the parents, and His displeasure is in their displeasure." [[Al-Tirmidhī narrated it from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr, who said: it was transmitted as a statement of his. Al-Bazzār narrated it and said: we know of no one who traced it back except Khālid ibn al-Ḥārith, and there is a matter to consider in this, because al-Ḥākim narrated it through the route of ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Mahdī from Shuʿba as a marfūʿ report; likewise al-Ṭabarānī and al-Bayhaqī narrated it through al-Qāsim ibn Salīm from Shuʿba as marfūʿ. Al-Bayhaqī also has it through al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Walīd from Shuʿba as marfūʿ. He said: we have also related it through Abū Isḥāq al-Fazārī, Zayd ibn Abī al-Rahhā and others as marfūʿ. The narration of Abū Isḥāq is in Abū Yaʿlā. Al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad said: Ādam ibn Abī Iyās narrated to us, Shuʿba narrated to us, and he mentioned it as mawqūf. Regarding this there is also a report from Ibn ʿUmar, narrated by al-Bazzār, who said: it was transmitted solely by ʿIṣma ibn Muḥammad al-Anṣārī from Yaḥyā ibn Saʿīd.]] " And it is narrated: "The one who is dutiful does whatever he wishes, and he will not enter the Fire; the one who is disobedient does whatever he wishes, and he will not enter Paradise." [[Al-Tha'labī narrated it through Muḥammad ibn al-Simmāk from ʿĀbid ibn Shurayḥ from ʿAṭā' from ʿĀ'isha. In its chain is Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Ghālib, Ghulām al-Khalīl, who is a liar. But Abū Nuʿaym narrated it in al-Ḥilya from another route, from Saḥnūn al-Simmāk, with the wording "for I will forgive you," and with the wording "for I will not forgive you."]] " Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated: "Indeed the dutiful does not die a bad death." A man said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "My parents have reached such old age that I attend to them as they attended to me in childhood; have I repaid them?" He said: "No, for they used to do that while they loved your remaining alive, but you do it while you wish for their death."

A man complained to the Messenger of Allah about his father, that he takes his wealth. He summoned the father, and there was an old man leaning on a staff. He asked him, and he said: "He was weak and I was strong, poor and I was rich, so I did not withhold anything of my wealth from him. Today I am weak and he is strong, I am poor and he is rich, and he stints me of his wealth." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wept and said: "There is no stone or clod that hears this but it weeps." Then he said to the son: "You and your wealth belong to your father; you and your wealth belong to your father." [[I have not found it. I say: it is narrated in Mu'jam al-Ṣaḥāba through a route.]] Another complained to him of the bad character of his mother, and he said [[I have not found it.]]: "Was she not of bad character when she carried you for nine months?" He said: "She was of bad character." He said: "Was she not like that when she nursed you for two years?" He said: "She was of bad character." He said: "Was she not like that when she stayed awake for you through her nights and went thirsty through her days?"

He said: "You have repaid her." He said: "What did I do?" He said: "You carried her on your shoulder for pilgrimage." He said: "You have not repaid her, not even a single birth pang." [[His words "not even a single birth pang": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, "al-ṭalq" is the pain of childbirth, so "ṭalqa" is one instance of it.]] It is related from Ibn ʿUmar that he saw a man in the circumambulation carrying his mother and saying:

"I am to her a mount that is not startled; when the riding-beasts take fright, she does not bolt.
What she carried and nursed me with is more; Allah, my Lord, is the Great, the Majestic."

[[Ibn ʿUmar recited this about a man carrying his mother on the Hajj. He likened himself to a mount, a eloquent simile, and "when the riding-beasts take fright" is an attribute of it, meaning that he is humbled toward her out of mercy, and does not tire of her as others do, for her carrying him and nursing him is more than his kindness to her. "Dhaʿara" (ذعر) like "taʿiba" (تعب): he feared and was alarmed, and what is meant is the necessary consequence of alarm and skittishness, which is distress and impatience and not allowing it to remain on his back. Then "Allahu akbar" was said, because it is the emblem of the Hajj from the day of sacrifice to the end of the days of tashrīq.]] "Do you think, O Ibn ʿUmar, that I have repaid her?" He said: "No, not even a single sigh." [[Ibn al-Mubārak narrated it in al-Birr wa-l-Ṣila: Sa'īd ibn Sa'īd ibn Abī Burda told us from his father, who said: Ibn ʿUmar used to circumambulate the House and saw a man, and he mentioned it. This is a sound chain. Al-Bayhaqī narrated it in al-Shuʿab in the fifty-fifth (section), and al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad narrated it abridged from Ādam from Saʿīd.]]

It is narrated from him (ﷺ): "Beware of disobedience to parents, for the scent of Paradise can be perceived from a distance of a thousand years, and the disobedient, the one who severs kinship, the old adulterer, and the one who drags his garment in arrogance will not smell it. Indeed greatness belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." [[Ibn ʿAdī narrated it through Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt from Abū Isḥāq from al-Ḥārith from ʿAlī, in these words and more complete, and in it "five hundred" instead of "a thousand." Al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Awsaṭ through Jābir al-Juʿfī from Abū Jaʿfar from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, with the wording "a thousand years." Jābir and Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt are both abandoned narrators.]]

The jurists said: one should not take one's father to a church, and if he sends for him to carry something, he should comply; he should not hand him wine, and he should take the vessel from him if he drinks it. It is narrated from Abū Yūsuf: if he orders him to light the fire beneath his pot in which there is pork, he may light it.

It is narrated from Ḥudhayfa that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to kill his father, who was in the ranks of the polytheists, and he said: "Leave him to someone else." [[I have not found it. It is not sound that Ḥudhayfa's father was in the ranks of the polytheists, for he was martyred at Uhud with the Muslims, killed by the hands of the Muslims by mistake, who thought him to be one of the disbelievers, as in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. But a story similar to the one mentioned is related for Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ.]]

Al-Faḍīl ibn ʿIyāḍ was asked about dutifulness to parents, and he said: "That you do not stand up to serve them out of laziness." Someone else was asked and said: "That you do not raise your voice over them, nor look at them with a sharp glance, and that they never see from you any opposition, outwardly or inwardly, and that you have mercy on them while they live and pray for them when they die, and that you serve their friends after them." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed among the greatest acts of righteousness is that a man keeps up ties with the friends of his father." [[Muslim narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, marfūʿ, and in it there is a story.]]
