He likened himself to a mount, a eloquent simile, and "when the riding-beasts take fright" is an attribute of it, meaning that he is humbled toward her out of mercy, and does not tire of her as others do, for her carrying him and nursing him is more than his kindness to her. "Dhaʿara" (ذعر) like "taʿiba" (تعب): he feared and was alarmed, and what is meant is the necessary consequence of alarm and skittishness, which is distress and impatience and not allowing it to remain on his back. Then "Allahu akbar" was said, because it is the emblem of the Hajj from the day of sacrifice to the end of the days of tashrīq.]] "Do you think, O Ibn ʿUmar, that I have repaid her?" He said: "No, not even a single sigh." [[Ibn al-Mubārak narrated it in al-Birr wa-l-Ṣila: Sa'īd ibn Sa'īd ibn Abī Burda told us from his father, who said: Ibn ʿUmar used to circumambulate the House and saw a man, and he mentioned it. This is a sound chain. Al-Bayhaqī narrated it in al-Shuʿab in the fifty-fifth (section), and al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad narrated it abridged from Ādam from Saʿīd.]]

It is narrated from him (ﷺ): "Beware of disobedience to parents, for the scent of Paradise can be perceived from a distance of a thousand years, and the disobedient, the one who severs kinship, the old adulterer, and the one who drags his garment in arrogance will not smell it. Indeed greatness belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds." [[Ibn ʿAdī narrated it through Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt from Abū Isḥāq from al-Ḥārith from ʿAlī, in these words and more complete, and in it "five hundred" instead of "a thousand." Al-Ṭabarānī narrated it in al-Awsaṭ through Jābir al-Juʿfī from Abū Jaʿfar from Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh, with the wording "a thousand years." Jābir and Muḥammad ibn al-Furāt are both abandoned narrators.]]

The jurists said: one should not take one's father to a church, and if he sends for him to carry something, he should comply; he should not hand him wine, and he should take the vessel from him if he drinks it. It is narrated from Abū Yūsuf: if he orders him to light the fire beneath his pot in which there is pork, he may light it.

It is narrated from Ḥudhayfa that he asked the Prophet (ﷺ) for permission to kill his father, who was in the ranks of the polytheists, and he said: "Leave him to someone else." [[I have not found it. It is not sound that Ḥudhayfa's father was in the ranks of the polytheists, for he was martyred at Uhud with the Muslims, killed by the hands of the Muslims by mistake, who thought him to be one of the disbelievers, as in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī. But a story similar to the one mentioned is related for Abū ʿUbayda ibn al-Jarrāḥ.]]

Al-Faḍīl ibn ʿIyāḍ was asked about dutifulness to parents, and he said: "That you do not stand up to serve them out of laziness." Someone else was asked and said: "That you do not raise your voice over them, nor look at them with a sharp glance, and that they never see from you any opposition, outwardly or inwardly, and that you have mercy on them while they live and pray for them when they die, and that you serve their friends after them." It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed among the greatest acts of righteousness is that a man keeps up ties with the friends of his father." [[Muslim narrated it from the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, marfūʿ, and in it there is a story.]]

Your Lord knows best what is in your souls: what is in your hearts of intention toward righteousness and dutifulness to your parents, and the conviction of the reverence due to them. ﴿If you are righteous﴾, intending uprightness and goodness, then if any lapse has come from you, in a state of anger, or when the breast is constricted, or from that which no human being is free of, or from the zeal of Islam, a slip that leads to harm to them, and then you turn back in repentance to God and seek His forgiveness for it, then ﴿indeed He is Forgiving to the awwābīn﴾, that is, to those who repent (tawwābīn). And it is narrated from Sa'īd ibn Jubayr: it refers to the hasty word that a man may utter to his father, intending nothing but good by it. And it is narrated from Sa'īd ibn al-Musayyab: the awwāb is the man who, whenever he commits a sin, hastens to repentance. It is also permissible that this be general for everyone from whom a wrong has come and who then repented of it, and included under it is the one who wronged his parents and repented of his wrongdoing, since it follows upon the same ruling (li-wurūdihi 'alā atharihi).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 26–27:

﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾: he enjoins the giving of rights to relatives other than parents, after enjoining it for the two of them. And "that they be given their rights": their right, if they are mahram (those with whom marriage is forbidden), such as parents and children, and if they are poor and unable to earn, and the man is well-off, is that he spend on them according to Abu Hanifa. And al-Shafi'i holds that maintenance is obligatory only for children and parents, and nothing more.

And if they are well-off, or if they are not mahram, such as paternal cousins, then their right is to keep ties with them through affection, visiting, good companionship, friendliness, standing by them in ease and hardship, supporting them, and the like. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: meaning, give these their right from the zakat. This is evidence that what is meant by the right given to the near of kin is that one attends to them with wealth. It has also been said: he meant by "the near of kin" the relatives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

*Tabdhir* (wasteful squandering): distributing wealth in what is not fitting, and spending it in an extravagant manner. In the Jahiliyya, people would slaughter their camels and gamble over them, and squander their wealth in boasting and showing off, and mention that in their poetry; so Allah commanded spending in its proper channels, that which brings one closer to Him and earns His favor. From Ibn Mas'ud: it is spending wealth in other than its due place. From Mujahid: "Even if one spends a mudd in falsehood, that is squandering." Some people spent a large sum on good works, and his companion said to him: "There is no good in extravagance." He replied: "There is no extravagance in good." From Abdullah ibn Amr: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by Sa'd while he was performing ablution, and said: "What is this extravagance, Sa'd?" He said: "Is there extravagance in ablution?" He said: "Yes, even if you are beside a flowing river." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi from his hadith. Its chain includes Ibn Lahi'a, who is weak.]]

﴿Brothers of the devils﴾: meaning, they are like them in wickedness, which is the utmost censure, since there is no evil greater than Satan's. Or they are their brothers and friends, because they obey them in what they command them of extravagance.

Or they are their companions in the Fire, as a warning. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: so he should not be obeyed, for he calls only to the like of his own deed. Al-Hasan recited: "ikhwan al-shayatin" (brothers of the devils).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 26–27:

﴿And give the near of kin his right﴾: he enjoins the giving of rights to relatives other than parents, after enjoining it for the two of them. And "that they be given their rights": their right, if they are mahram (those with whom marriage is forbidden), such as parents and children, and if they are poor and unable to earn, and the man is well-off, is that he spend on them according to Abu Hanifa. And al-Shafi'i holds that maintenance is obligatory only for children and parents, and nothing more.

And if they are well-off, or if they are not mahram, such as paternal cousins, then their right is to keep ties with them through affection, visiting, good companionship, friendliness, standing by them in ease and hardship, supporting them, and the like. ﴿And the needy and the wayfarer﴾: meaning, give these their right from the zakat. This is evidence that what is meant by the right given to the near of kin is that one attends to them with wealth. It has also been said: he meant by "the near of kin" the relatives of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

*Tabdhir* (wasteful squandering): distributing wealth in what is not fitting, and spending it in an extravagant manner. In the Jahiliyya, people would slaughter their camels and gamble over them, and squander their wealth in boasting and showing off, and mention that in their poetry; so Allah commanded spending in its proper channels, that which brings one closer to Him and earns His favor. From Ibn Mas'ud: it is spending wealth in other than its due place. From Mujahid: "Even if one spends a mudd in falsehood, that is squandering." Some people spent a large sum on good works, and his companion said to him: "There is no good in extravagance." He replied: "There is no extravagance in good." From Abdullah ibn Amr: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed by Sa'd while he was performing ablution, and said: "What is this extravagance, Sa'd?" He said: "Is there extravagance in ablution?" He said: "Yes, even if you are beside a flowing river." [[Narrated by Ibn Majah, Ahmad, Abu Ya'la and al-Bayhaqi from his hadith. Its chain includes Ibn Lahi'a, who is weak.]]

﴿Brothers of the devils﴾: meaning, they are like them in wickedness, which is the utmost censure, since there is no evil greater than Satan's. Or they are their brothers and friends, because they obey them in what they command them of extravagance.

Or they are their companions in the Fire, as a warning. ﴿And Satan has ever been ungrateful to his Lord﴾: so he should not be obeyed, for he calls only to the like of his own deed. Al-Hasan recited: "ikhwan al-shayatin" (brothers of the devils).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 28:

﴿And if you turn away from them while seeking mercy from your Lord, which you hope for, then speak to them a gentle word﴾ (﴿وإن أعرضت عن ذى القربى والمسكين وابن السبيل حياء من الردّ فَقُلْ لَهُمْ قَوْلًا مَيْسُوراً﴾). Then do not leave them unanswered when they ask you. The Prophet (ﷺ) [[Narrated by Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim from Anas: "The Prophet (ﷺ) would never be asked for anything except that he gave it or remained silent," and there is a story in it. In al-Tabarani's al-Awsat, from Ali (may Allah be pleased with him): "When the Prophet (ﷺ) was asked for something and he intended to do it, he said: 'Yes.' And when he intended not to do it, he remained silent and never said 'No' to anything." Then he mentioned a story. Its chain is weak.]] when he was asked for something he did not have, would turn away from the questioner and remain silent out of shyness.

As for His saying ﴿ابْتِغاءَ رَحْمَةٍ مِنْ رَبِّكَ﴾ (seeking mercy from your Lord): it may be connected to the answer of the conditional, placed before it, meaning: "Then speak to them a gentle, easy word, and promise them a good promise, as mercy for them and to comfort their hearts, seeking mercy from your Lord," i.e., seek the mercy of Allah which you hope for through your mercy towards them. Or it may be connected to the condition, meaning: "And if you turn away from them because of the lack of provision from your Lord, which you hope will be opened to you," so He called the provision "mercy," and "fa-radduhum radan jamilan" (so refuse them graciously). Here the seeking (ibtigha') is placed in the position of the lack (fuqd), because the one who lacks provision is one who seeks it, so the lack was the cause of the seeking and the seeking was caused by it; thus the effect was put in the place of the cause.

It is also permissible that the meaning of ﴿وَإِمَّا تُعْرِضَنَّ عَنْهُمُ﴾ is: even if you do not benefit them and do not relieve their want, due to being unable to do so. "Turning away" is not meant literally as turning the face, but as a metaphor for turning away from that, because the one who refuses to give turns his face away. It is said: "yasara al-amr wa 'asura" (the matter became easy or difficult), like "sa'ada al-rajul wa nahasa" (the man became fortunate or unfortunate), so ﴿مَيْسُوراً﴾ is a passive participle (maf'ul). It was also said that its meaning is: "Say to them: May Allah grant us and you of His bounty," as a supplication for them that He ease their poverty, as if the meaning were: "a word that has ease (dhu maysur), which is ease (al-yusr)," i.e., a supplication containing ease.

[[Note on "like sa'ada al-rajul wa nahasa": in al-Sihah: sa'ada al-rajul bi'l-kasr fa-huwa sa'id, like salima fa-huwa salim; wa sa'ada bi'l-damm fa-huwa mas'ud. (A)]] [[Note on "a word that has ease (dhu maysur), which is ease": in al-Sihah: al-ma'sur is the opposite of al-maysur, and both are verbal nouns. Sibawayh said: they are two adjectives. (A)]]

This is an illustration of the withholding of the miser and the giving of the spendthrift, and a command to moderation (*iqtisad*), which lies between extravagance (*israf*) and stinginess (*taqtir*). ﴿So you sit down blameworthy﴾, meaning you become blameworthy before God, because the spendthrift is displeasing to Him and to people. The needy say: "He gave to so-and-so and deprived me." The wealthy say: "He does not manage his livelihood well." And you are blamed in your own estimation.

When you are in need and regret what you have done, ﴿ruined﴾ (*mahsur*), cut off, with nothing in your possession. The word *hasir* is used of one whose travel has worn him out, and of one who has been worn down by begging.

It is narrated from Jabir that while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sitting, a boy came to him and said: "My mother asks you to clothe her." He said: "From one time to another; it will appear. Come back to us." The boy went to his mother, and she said: "Tell him: my mother asks you for the garment you are wearing." So he entered his house, removed his shirt, gave it to the boy, and sat naked. Bilal called the adhan, and they waited, but he did not come out for the prayer. [[I have not found it]].

It is also said that he gave al-Aqra' ibn Habis one hundred camels, and ʿUyayna ibn Hisn [[The phrase "one hundred camels and ʿUyayna ibn Hisn" probably has a missing part after it, its intended meaning being: one hundred.]]. ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas came and recited:

*Do you place my share and the share of the slaves between ʿUyayna and al-Aqra'?*
*Neither Hisn nor Habis*
*Would excel my grandfather in an assembly.*
*I was not inferior to either of them,*
*And whoever is lowered today will not be raised.*

[[For al-ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas, may God be pleased with him, addressing the Prophet (ﷺ). It is narrated that he gave each of al-Aqra' ibn Habis and ʿUyayna ibn Hisn one hundred camels to win their hearts (*ta'lif al-qulub*). ʿAbbas recited this, and Abu Bakr raised it to the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Cut off his tongue from me." People were alarmed, and so were some others. He had intended to give him in order to win his heart as well. The interrogative is for expressing wonder.

It may also be for denial, but that is far-fetched from a Companion. That is: "Do you divide my share and the share of the slaves between these two, when their fathers did not excel my father, Mirdas, [the noun is kept from *sarf* due to necessity (*li-l-darura*)]." The word *al-ʿabid* may be read as a diminutive (*musaghghar*), and in place of it the text may read *jaddi* (my grandfather), and "*shaykhi fi majma*" (my elder in an assembly), meaning an assembly of war. I am no less than either of them, so we are equal in origin and branch, so how are we now differentiated? Moreover, whoever is lowered in rank will not be raised in status. It is also narrated as *minhumu*, meaning "of the four." It is narrated as *wa-man yukhfad*, in the passive voice. The mention of Hisn and Habis after ʿUyayna and al-Aqra' is an example of *laff wa-nashr* (the rhetorical device of arranged enumeration) in order.]]

He said: "O Abu Bakr, cut off his tongue from me. Give him one hundred camels." [[Muslim narrated it from the narration of ʿUtba ibn Rifaʿa ibn Rafiʿ, from Rafiʿ ibn Khadij, who said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) gave Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, Safwan ibn Umayya, ʿUyayna ibn Hisn, and al-Aqra' ibn Habis each one hundred camels.

ʿAbbas ibn Mirdas was given less than that. ʿAbbas said, and recited the poem. He said: 'The Messenger of God (ﷺ) completed one hundred for him.'" Ibn Ishaq also narrated it in *al-Maghazi*, saying: "ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Hazm and others narrated to me," and mentioned the story, and at its end he said: "Be wary, and cut off his tongue." So they increased it until he was satisfied. Likewise, Musa ibn ʿUqba, al-Waqidi, and Ibn Saʿd mentioned it, and in none of their chains is it said that the one who addressed him this way was Abu Bakr.]] Then this verse was revealed.

Then He consoled the Messenger of God (ﷺ) concerning what burdened him of the (people's) importuning, telling him that this is not because of any contempt on your part before Him, nor because of any stinginess toward you, but because His will in the extension of provisions and their measure (qadarahā) follows wisdom and benefit.

[[His words "fi basti al-arzaq wa qadarihā," meaning their restriction (tadyiqihā). So reports al-Sihah. (ʿA)]]

It is also permissible that he intends that expansion and restriction are only from the command of God, in whose hand are the treasuries; as for the servants, they must be moderate. It is possible that the Mighty and Exalted, when He extends to His servants or restricts (them), observes the middle of the two states: He does not carry the one to whom He extends (provision) to the utmost of his desire, nor the one upon whom He restricts (provision) to the utmost of his harm. So follow His practice.

Their killing their children: this is their burying their daughters [[His words "this is their burying their daughters": wa'd al-bint (burying a girl) means burying her in the grave while she is alive, as in al-Sihah. (Ṭ)]], they used to bury them alive out of fear of poverty, which is destitution (al-imlaq). So God forbade them and guaranteed their provision.

It is read khashyata with a kasra on the kha'. It is also read khiṭan, which means sin (al-ithm); one says khati'a khaṭa'an, like atham ithman, and khaṭa'an, which is the opposite of correct (al-ṣawab), a noun from akhṭa'a. It was said that khiṭʾ and khaṭʾ are like al-ḥidhr and al-ḥadhr. Also khiṭā' with a kasra and a long vowel, khaṭā' with a fatḥa and a long vowel, and khaṭa' with a fatḥa and a sukūn. From al-Ḥasan: khaṭā with a fatḥa, dropping the hamza, like al-khabb. From Abu Rajā': with a kasra on the kha', not hamzated.

Fāḥisha (an abomination): something ugly, exceeding the limit of ugliness. Wa-sā'a sabīla (and evil is the way): an evil path, its path, namely that you seize from another his wife, his sister, or his daughter without any cause, when a cause is available, which is al-ṣihr (affinity by marriage) that God has prescribed [[His saying "which is al-ṣihr that God has prescribed": that is, marriage. Stated by al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon). (ʿA)]].

Except for a just cause (إلا بالحق). That is, only in one of three cases: that you disbelieve (إلا بأن تكفر), or that you kill a believer deliberately, or that you commit adultery after having been married (إحصان). ﴿Wrongfully slain﴾ (مَظْلُوماً), not riding any one of these, ﴿to his heir﴾ (لِوَلِيِّهِ), the one who has between him and the slain a kinship that obliges him to demand his blood. If he has no heir, then the authority (السلطان) is his heir (وليه), ﴿an authority﴾ (سُلْطاناً), a power to exact retribution from the killer. Or a proof by which he may prevail over him. ﴿So let him not commit excess﴾ (فَلا يُسْرِفْ): the pronoun refers to the heir. That is: he should not kill other than the killer, nor two when the killer is one, as was the custom of the Jahiliyya: if one of them was killed, they would kill a group in return for him. Thus Muhalhil said when Bujayr ibn al-Harith ibn Abbad was killed:

﴿Pay with the sandal-thong of Kulayb﴾ (بؤ بشسع نعل كليب). [[His saying "bu' bi-sha' na'l Kulayb": in al-Sihah, one says "bu'a bihi," meaning "be among those who are to be killed in exchange for him." Al-bawa' means equivalence. Al-sha' is one of the thongs of a sandal that are tied to its strap. Al-ghurra means a slave or a female slave. (ʿ)]] And he said:

﴿Every slain man in Kulayb is a ghurra, until death reaches the family of Murra﴾ (كُلُّ قَتِيلٍ فِى كُلَيْبٍ غُرَّهْ ... حَتَّي يَنَالَ الْقَتْلُ آلَ مُرَّهْ). [[Al-ghurra: the lowly, meaning: every slain man we have killed in this tribe is not an equal to those of ours who killed him, until our killing reaches the family of Murra, who are his equal.]]

And they would kill other than the killer when there was no equivalence. It has been said: the excess is mutilation. Abu Muslim, the author of al-Dawla, read: ﴿fa-la yusrif﴾ with a nominative ending, as a report with the meaning of a command, and there is an emphasis in it that is not present in the imperative. From Mujahid: the pronoun refers to the first killer. It was also read: ﴿fa-la tusrif﴾, addressed to the heir or to the killer of the wronged one.

In the reading of Ubayy: ﴿fa-la tusrifu﴾, returning to ﴿and do not kill﴾. ﴿Indeed he is supported﴾ (إِنَّهُ كانَ مَنْصُوراً): the pronoun may refer to the heir, meaning: it is enough for him that God has supported him by making retribution obligatory for him, and that God has supported him [[His saying "wa-bi-anna Allah qad nasarahu" is perhaps "aw anna." (ʿ)]] with the aid of the authority and by the believers' backing in exacting the right, so let him not seek beyond his right. Or it may refer to the wronged one, because God supports him, since He made retribution obligatory for his killing, and He supports him in the Hereafter with reward. Or to the one whom the heir kills without right and exceeds in killing him, for he is supported by the obligation of retribution upon the one who exceeds.

with the way that is best: that is, the manner or quality that is best, namely preserving it and making it fruitful. Indeed the covenant was something to be asked about (مَسْؤُلًا), i.e. something demanded (مطلوبا), which the one who made the covenant is asked to keep and fulfil, not to waste.

[[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "i.e., the one who made the covenant is asked to fulfil it and not break it... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "This is a good statement, except for the word takhyil (personification/imaginative representation), since its rejection of it has already been mentioned, and it should be replaced with tamthil (figurative representation). The first interpretation is the apparent one, and the preposition 'anhu (about it), which is the genitive, is omitted for lightness. It is mentioned in another verse: ﴿Each of those, it was asked about﴾ (kullu ula'ika kana 'anhu mas'ula, 17:36). And it supports the interpretation that the covenant itself is asked, in the manner of a figure of speech, the standing of the womb before God and its being asked about whoever joined it and whoever severed it. This is reported in the authentic hadith. And God is the Granter of success."]]

It is also permissible that this is a personification (takhyil): as if it is said to the covenant, "Why did you break? Why did you not fulfil [your obligation] to him?" as a rebuke to the one who broke it, just as one says to the buried infant girl, "For what sin were you killed?" It is also permissible that what is meant is that the party to the covenant was the one who would be asked.

It was also read as bi-l-qisṭās (with a ḍamma and with a kasra), and it is al-qarasṭūn (a steelyard, a type of balance). It has been said: every balance, whether small or large, of the balances for dirhams or other things. And aḥsanu ta'wīlan (﴿and better in outcome﴾): better in consequence. It is on the pattern of taf'īl, from āla, meaning "to return," and it is what something returns to, its outcome.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 36:

﴿And do not pursue﴾ (wa-la taqfu wa-la tattabi‘). It is also read: wa-la taqfu. It is said: qafa athrahu and qafawahu (he followed his trail), and from this comes al-qafah (the trackers, those who follow footprints). The meaning is: do not, in your pursuit, follow what you have no knowledge of, whether in speech or in action, like one who follows a path without knowing that it will lead him to his destination, so he is astray. The intended meaning is the prohibition against a man saying what he does not know, and acting on what he does not know. It also enters, quite evidently, the prohibition against taqlid (blind imitation), because it is following what one does not know to be sound or unsound. It is related from Ibn al-Hanafiyyah: "false testimony." It is related from al-Hasan: "Do not accuse (taqfu) your Muslim brother when he passes by you, saying: 'This one does such-and-such, I saw him doing it, I heard him,' when you have not seen it, even if you have only heard it." It is also said: al-qafw is similar to al-‘udhayhah (slander). From this is the hadith: "Whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, Allah will confine him in radghat al-khabal (the mire of corruption) until he brings forth the way out of it." [Footnote: "Radghat al-khabal": in the Sihah, al-radghah (with a vowel on the ra) is water, mud and severe mire; and al-khabal is hardship and corruption. The version in the hadith "whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, Allah will hold him (waqafahu) in radghat al-khabal until he brings forth the way out of it, and it is said: it is the pus of the people of the Fire."] until he comes with the way out. [Footnote: I have not seen this wording traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a marfu‘ report. Abu ‘Ubayd mentioned it in al-Gharib as a saying of Hassan ibn ‘Atiyyah, saying: "Muhammad ibn Kathir narrated to us from al-Awza‘i from him with this." Ahmad and al-Tabarani related, through Mu‘adh ibn Anas, a report traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever accuses a believer of what is not in him, intending to disgrace him with it, Allah will hold him on the bridge of Hell until he comes out of what he said." In Musnad al-Shamiyyin of al-Tabarani, through Mutar al-Warraq from ‘Ata’ al-Khurasani from Nafi‘ from Ibn ‘Umar: "Whoever slanders a believing man or woman will be detained in radghat al-khabal until he brings the way out." It is in Abu Dawud from the narration of Yahya ibn Rashid from Ibn ‘Umar with the wording: "Whoever says about a believer what is not in him, Allah will settle him in radghat al-khabal until he brings the way out, and he comes out of what he said." Al-Hakim also reported it from the hadith of ‘Abdullah ibn ‘Amr ibn al-‘As, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever says about a believer what is not in him, Allah will confine him in radghat al-khabal until he brings the way out."]] And he recited:

﻿*And like the statues, of high noses, dwells modesty among them; they do not spread the slander (taqafi).*

[Footnote: He describes women as beautiful like statues (sing. dumyah, an idol or a figure of ivory inlaid with jewels). Shumm is the plural of shamma'; and al-‘aranin are the noses, meaning high-held noses, a metaphor for their nobility and elevated rank. Or it is a metaphor for their being noble free women, since lowered noses are characteristic of slaves and servants. He likened them to houses. He likened modesty to a people who dwell in them, by way of metaphor (al-makniyyah), and "dwelling" is an imaginative depiction (takhyil) of this; it is a metaphor and an exaggeration of modesty's constant presence with them. "They do not spread": i.e., they do not display taqafi, that is, pursuing with slander, from qafawtuhu when one follows him with backbiting. In "spreading it" there is a metaphor for negating it, since it exists only between two or more.]] That is, mutual slander. And al-Kumayt said:

*And I do not shoot the innocent without a sin, nor do I pursue the chaste women if they are pursued.*

[Footnote: One says: the woman was chaste (hasanat, hasina) and is chaste (hasin, hasna', hassan), meaning she is virtuous. Al-hawasin is the plural of hasin. He says: I do not accuse the innocent of a false charge, but only of a proven sin. Apparently this is in the sense of an exception that is disjunct (istithna' munqati‘), since the innocent, as long as he is innocent, has no sin, and I do not follow chaste women and speak of them with indecency as long as they are chaste, even if people pursue them and talk about them; so how much more so when no one speaks of them?]] This has been used as evidence by one who rejects ijtihad, but this is not sound, because it is a kind of knowledge; the Law has made dominant assumption (ghalib al-zann) stand in the place of knowledge and has commanded acting upon it. ﴿Each of those﴾ (ula'ika) refers to hearing, sight and heart, as in the verse:

*Were it not for the watchfulness of eyes, we would have seen them: the gazelle-like eyes of the wild cows and the flowing necks of the gazelles.*

[Footnote: This is a poem of Jarir ibn ‘Atiyyah addressing himself by way of tajrid (the device of addressing oneself as another). He says: were it not for the women's watching of the eyes, i.e., the watchful spies who look at us, they would have shown themselves to us and displayed their eyes, which are like the eyes of wild cattle. "Maqlu al-maha" is a clear metaphor, and so is "sawalif al-aram." Al-salifah is the front of the neck and its surface. Al-aram is the plural of ram (a white gazelle), and its origin is "aram" with a long hamza after the ra', on the pattern of ahmal, which was changed to what precedes it. It may also be the plural of rim (with a fatha), the white gazelle, so it was hamzated and changed. "Hal" here means "qad" or is for confirmation: that is, does she forbid you from them, the killing of Murraqish, the famous lover? Or their action toward ‘Urwah, also a lover. Al-Liwa is a specific place of twisted sand; and "blame the whole of life after our life in those days" or "blame the entire duration of life after those former days," and he referred to it with the form used for rational beings because of its greatness to him, and because restricting it to rational beings is a later usage. It is also possible that "ba‘d" is a time adverb for the dwellings and the life. Some grammarians made "dhamm" passive, and what follows it is its substitute as subject.]] and it is said of ﴿the hearing﴾ (al-sam‘) in the place of the subject: each of them was asked about, so "mas’ul" is attributed to the preposition-phrase, like "al-maghdub" in His words ﴿not of those who have earned anger﴾. It is said to a person: why did you hear what it was not lawful for you to hear, why did you look at what it was not lawful for you to look at, why did you resolve upon what it was not lawful for you to resolve upon? It is also read: wa-l-fu’ada with fatha on the fa' and the waw; the hamza was changed to waw after the damma in al-fu’ad, and then the heart kept the fatha.

*maraḥan* (مَرَحاً) is a *ḥāl* (a circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject), meaning: possessing exultation (ḏā maraḥ).

It is also read مَرَحاً. Al-Akhfash preferred the verbal noun (*maṣdar*) over the active participle (*ism al-fāʿil*) because of the emphasis it carries.

﴿لَنْ تَخْرِقَ الْأَرْضَ﴾ means: you will never make a hole in the earth, that is, you will never make holes in it.

[[Al-Zamakhsharī said: "Its meaning is: you will never make holes in it..." etc. Aḥmad said: In this there is mockery and rebuke sufficient to deter whoever habitually walks in this manner. God has preserved the common people of our time from this gait, but our reciters and jurists have fallen into it. One of them, once he has learned two issues, or has seated students before him, or has tasted a little of worldly leadership, struts in his walk and swaggers, and does not consider that he is rivalling the mountains; rather he rubs his crown against the vault of heaven. They pass over the Qur'an while turning away from it. What benefit is it to him to recite the Qur'an or to have it recited to him, when his heart is far from reflecting upon it? And God is the Guardian of success.]]

by your treading upon it and the severity of your footfall.

It is also read لَنْ تَخْرُقَ with a ḍammah on the rāʾ (*tukhruqa*).

﴿وَلَنْ تَبْلُغَ الْجِبالَ طُولًا﴾ means: nor will you ever reach the mountains in height, by your swagger. This is a mockery of the arrogant person.

It is read سَيِّئَةً and سَيِّئُهُ, the latter being the adjective *sayyiʾ* in construct with the pronoun referring to *kull* (each). It is also read سيئاً in some codices (*maṣāḥif*), and سيئات (*sayyiʾāt*). In the reading of Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, may Allah be pleased with him: كان شأنه.

If you ask: how is it said سَيِّئَةً when He says مَكْرُوهاً (disliked)? I answer: *al-sayyiʾah* functions as a noun, in the same position as *al-dhanb* (sin) and *al-ithm* (sin), and it has lost the sense of an adjective, so its feminine marking is not taken into account. There is no difference between one who reads سيئة and one who reads سيئاً. Do you not see that you say: adultery is an evil deed (*sayyiʾah*), just as you say: theft is an evil deed? So you do not distinguish between attributing it to a masculine or a feminine noun.

If you ask: among the qualities mentioned, some are evil and some good, which is why whoever reads سَيِّئُهُ with the genitive construction reads it that way; so what is the justification for whoever reads سيئة? I answer: all of that is a comprehensive reference to what He has forbidden in particular, not to all the qualities enumerated.

This is al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 17, verse 39:

"That" refers to what preceded it, from His saying ﴿Do not set up another god along with Allah﴾ up to this point. He called it wisdom (hikmah) because it is a firm, sound statement into which corruption can find no entry in any way. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: "These eighteen verses were in the tablets of Musa, the first of them being ﴿Do not set up another god along with Allah﴾." Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And We wrote for him on the tablets concerning everything an admonition﴾, and it is ten verses in the Torah. Allah made its opening and its closing the prohibition of shirk, because tawhid is the head of all wisdom and its foundation. Whoever lacks it, his wisdom and knowledge will not benefit him, even if he surpasses the wise in them [[His saying "even if he surpasses the wise in them": in al-Sihah, "badhahu" means he overcame him and outdid him. (ʿ)]] and strikes the sky with his forehead. The volumes of wisdom did not avail the philosophers, and they are more misguided about the religion of Allah than cattle.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 40:

"Afa-asfakum" (Has your Lord then favoured you) is an address to those who said, "The angels are the daughters of God." The hamza (interrogative particle) here expresses denial. The meaning is: has your Lord singled you out, in purity and exclusivity, with the best of offspring, namely sons, withholding no share of them for Himself, while taking for Himself the inferior ones, which are daughters? This contradicts wisdom and what your own reason and customs accept, for slaves are not given the finest and purest of things, unmixed with impurity, while the lowest and most inferior is reserved for their masters. "Innakum lataqooloona qawlan 'atheeman" (Indeed you utter a monstrous saying): by attributing offspring to Him, which belong only to bodies; then by preferring yourselves over Him, since you assign to Him what you dislike; and then by making the angels, who are the highest and most noble of God's creation [[The phrase "they are the highest and most noble of God's creation" follows the position of the Mu'tazila. As for the Ahl al-Sunna, some humans are superior to angels. (ʿA.)]], the inferior of God's creation, namely females.

And indeed We have diversified (ṣarrafnā) in this Qur'an [that which is] to be taken as meaning that this Qur'an aims at nullifying their attribution of daughters to Allah, since it is among the things He has varied and repeated mention of. The meaning would be: "And indeed We have varied the discourse on this theme." Or: We made variation occur in it and made it a place for repetition. It is also permissible that by "this Qur'an" he indicates the revelation (tanzīl), and that He intends: "And indeed We have varied it," meaning this theme, in various passages of the revelation, so the pronoun is omitted because it is known. It is also read ṣarrafnā with the lighter (takhfīf) pronunciation, and likewise li-yadhdhakarū is read both with doubling (tashdīd) and without (takhfīf), meaning: We repeated it so that they might be admonished, take heed, and be reassured by what is put forward as proof against them; but it increases them only in aversion (nufūran) from the truth and in lack of reassurance toward it. It is reported from Sufyān that when he recited it he would say: "It increases me in submission to You, just as it increases Your enemies in aversion."

Recited with both the ta' and the ya' (as you say, "kamā taqūlūn"). The word idhan indicates that what follows it, namely la-ibtaghaw, is the answer to the claim of the polytheists and the response (jaza') to "law" (if). The meaning of la-ibtaghaw ila dhi al-ʿarsh sabilan is: they would have sought a way to the One who possesses dominion and lordship, by contention, as kings do with one another, as in His saying: "Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted" [21:22]. It was also said: they would have sought nearness to Him, as in His saying: "Those whom they call upon seek the means of access to their Lord" [17:57].

ʿUluwwan (exalted) is in the sense of taʿalaya (exalted far above). What is intended is clearing Him of that and declaring Him free from it. The meaning of describing the exaltation as "great" (kabīr) is an intensification in the sense of disassociation and distance from what they ascribe to Him.

ʿUluwwan (exalted) is in the sense of taʿalaya (exalted far above). What is intended is clearing Him of that and declaring Him free from it. The meaning of describing the exaltation as "great" (kabīr) is an intensification in the sense of disassociation and distance from what they ascribe to Him.

The meaning is: they glorify Him through the tongue of the state (*lisan al-hal*), insofar as they point to the Creator (*al-Sani'*), and through His power and wisdom. It is as though they speak by that means and as though they declare God, exalted and mighty is He, free of what is impermissible for Him, such as partners and other things.

If you ask: what do you make of His words ﴿but you do not understand their glorification﴾, when this glorification is understood and known? I answer: the address is to the polytheists. Although, when asked about the Creator of the heavens and the earth, they would say, "God," yet because they made other gods alongside Him despite their acknowledgment, it is as though they had neither reflected nor affirmed. For the outcome of sound reflection and firm affirmation is contrary to what they were upon. So when they did not understand the glorification and did not seek clarity about the indication of the Creator, they are described as not understanding it.

If you ask: those in them glorify Him in reality, and they are the angels and the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), and they are conjoined with the heavens and the earth, so what is the justification for this? I answer: the figurative glorification is present in all of them, so it was obligatory to take the word in that sense. Otherwise, a single word in a single state would be taken both literally and figuratively.

﴿Indeed He is ever Forbearing and Forgiving﴾, in that He does not hasten to punish you for your heedlessness, your poor reflection, your ignorance of the glorification, and your association of partners with Him.

﴿حِجاباً مَسْتُوراً﴾: ذا ستر، كقولهم. ﴿سَيْلاً مَفْعَماً﴾: ذو إفعام. وقيل: هو حجاب لا يُرى، فهو مستور. ويجوز أن يُراد أنه حجاب، من دونه حجاب أو حُجُب، فهو مستور بغيره. أو حجاب يستر أن يُبصَر، فكيف يُبصِر المحتجَبُ به؟

وهذه حكاية لما كانوا يقولونه: ﴿وَقالُوا قُلُوبُنا فِي أَكِنَّةٍ مِمَّا تَدْعُونا إِلَيْهِ وَفِي آذانِنا وَقْرٌ وَمِنْ بَيْنِنا وَبَيْنِكَ حِجابٌ﴾. كأنه قال: وإذا قرأتَ القرآنَ جعلنا على زعمهم ﴿أَنْ يَفْقَهُوهُ﴾، كراهةَ أن يفقهوه. أو لأنّ قوله: ﴿وَجَعَلْنا عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ أَكِنَّةً﴾ فيه معنى المنع من الفقه، فكأنه قيل: ومنعناهم أن يفقهوه.

يقال: وحد يحد وحدا وحدة، نحو: وعد يعد وعدا وعدة. و﴿وَحْدَهُ﴾ من باب رجع، عوده على بدئه، وافعله جهدك وطاقتك. وفي أنه مصدر سادّ مسدّ الحال، أصله: يحد وحده، بمعنى واحدا، وحده.

والنفور: مصدر بمعنى التولية، أو جمع نافر كقاعد وقعود، أي: يحبون أن تُذكر معه آلهتهم، لأنهم مشركون، فإذا سمعوا بالتوحيد نفروا. ﴿بِما يَسْتَمِعُونَ بِهِ﴾ من الهزؤ بك وبالقرآن، ومن اللغو: كان يقوم عن يمينه إذا قرأ، رجلان من عبد الدار، ورجلان منهم عن يساره، فيصفقون ويصفرون ويخلطون عليه بالأشعار.

و﴿بِهِ﴾ في موضع الحال، كما تقول: يستمعون بالهزؤ، أي: هازئين.

﴿إِذْ يَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ نصب بـ(أعلم)، أي: أعلم وقت استماعهم بما به يستمعون. ﴿وَإِذْ هُمْ نَجْوى﴾ وبما يتناجون به، إذ هم ذو نجوى. ﴿إِذْ يَقُولُ﴾ بدل من ﴿إِذْ هُمْ﴾. ﴿مَسْحُوراً﴾: سُحر فجُنّ. وقيل: هو من السحر، وهو الرئة، أي: هو بشر مثلكم.

﴿ضَرَبُوا لَكَ الْأَمْثالَ﴾: مثّلوك بالشاعر والساحر والمجنون. ﴿فَضَلُّوا﴾ في جميع ذلك، ضلالَ من يطلب في التيه طريقاً يسلكه فلا يقدر عليه، فهو متحيّر في أمره لا يدري ما يصنع.

وهذه حكاية لما كانوا يقولونه: ﴿وَقالُوا قُلُوبُنا فِي أَكِنَّةٍ مِمَّا تَدْعُونا إِلَيْهِ وَفِي آذانِنا وَقْرٌ وَمِنْ بَيْنِنا وَبَيْنِكَ حِجابٌ﴾. كأنه قال: وإذا قرأتَ القرآنَ جعلنا على زعمهم ﴿أَنْ يَفْقَهُوهُ﴾، كراهةَ أن يفقهوه. أو لأنّ قوله: ﴿وَجَعَلْنا عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ أَكِنَّةً﴾ فيه معنى المنع من الفقه، فكأنه قيل: ومنعناهم أن يفقهوه.

يقال: وحد يحد وحدا وحدة، نحو: وعد يعد وعدا وعدة. و﴿وَحْدَهُ﴾ من باب رجع، عوده على بدئه، وافعله جهدك وطاقتك. وفي أنه مصدر سادّ مسدّ الحال، أصله: يحد وحده، بمعنى واحدا، وحده.

والنفور: مصدر بمعنى التولية، أو جمع نافر كقاعد وقعود، أي: يحبون أن تُذكر معه آلهتهم، لأنهم مشركون، فإذا سمعوا بالتوحيد نفروا. ﴿بِما يَسْتَمِعُونَ بِهِ﴾ من الهزؤ بك وبالقرآن، ومن اللغو: كان يقوم عن يمينه إذا قرأ، رجلان من عبد الدار، ورجلان منهم عن يساره، فيصفقون ويصفرون ويخلطون عليه بالأشعار.

و﴿بِهِ﴾ في موضع الحال، كما تقول: يستمعون بالهزؤ، أي: هازئين.

﴿إِذْ يَسْتَمِعُونَ﴾ نصب بـ(أعلم)، أي: أعلم وقت استماعهم بما به يستمعون. ﴿وَإِذْ هُمْ نَجْوى﴾ وبما يتناجون به، إذ هم ذو نجوى. ﴿إِذْ يَقُولُ﴾ بدل من ﴿إِذْ هُمْ﴾. ﴿مَسْحُوراً﴾: سُحر فجُنّ. وقيل: هو من السحر، وهو الرئة، أي: هو بشر مثلكم.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 49–51:

When they said: "Shall we indeed, when we are bones, be raised up as a new creation?" it was said to them: "Be you stones or iron," so that his (God's) answer, "Be you," corresponds to their saying, "we were." It is as if it were said: "Be stones or iron, and do not be bones, for He is able to bring you back to life." The meaning is: you consider it far-fetched that God should renew your creation and return you to the state of life and the moistness and freshness of the living, after you were dry bones. Yet bones are part of the parts of a living being; indeed they are the pillar of its creation upon which the rest is built. So it is no marvel that God, by His power, should return them to their original state. But even if you were the thing furthest from life and the moistness of the living, and of the same substance as that from which man is composed, namely dry stones or iron (although their nature is hardness and firmness), He would be able to return you to the state of life, "or a creation of what is greater in your breasts" (aw khalqan mimma yakburu fi sudurikum), that is, or a creation of what is, in your estimation, too great to accept life and which, in your opinion, is too grand for the Creator to revive; yet He will revive it. It has also been said: what is greater in their breasts is death. It has also been said: the heavens and the earth. "They will shake their heads at you" (fasayunghiduna), that is, they will move them toward you in wonder and mockery.

"They will shake their heads at you" (fasayunghiduna), that is, they will move them toward you in wonder and mockery.

The call and the response are both figurative. The meaning is: on the day He calls you, you will rise up, submissive and compliant, without resisting. His saying ﴿with His praise﴾ is a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) describing them, meaning "praising," and it is an intensification of their compliance with the resurrection. It is like when you order someone to ride an animal that is difficult for him, and he resists and refuses, so you say, "You will ride it while praising and thanking [Him]," meaning: you will be driven onto it and forced, until you become gentle, like a docile (musmaḥ) [[The word "musmaḥ" in al-Sihah (the lexicon of al-Jawhari): "asmaḥat qarunatuhu," meaning his disposition submitted and he followed the matter. (ʿ)]] one who is eager for it and praises him for it. From Saʿid ibn Jubayr: they shake the dust from their heads and say, "Glory be to You, O Allah, and praise be to You." ﴿And you will think﴾ and see the terror, so in that moment you will consider the length of your stay in the world to be short, and you will imagine it to have been a day or part of a day. From Qatada: the world became insignificant in their eyes when they witnessed the Hereafter.

And say to My servants: say to the believers that they should speak to the polytheists in the word that is best and gentlest, and not be harsh with them, like His saying: "And argue with them in the way that is best" [16:125]. He explained "the way that is best" by His saying: "Your Lord knows you best. If He wills, He will have mercy on you, or if He wills, He will punish you" [17:54]. That is, they should say to them this word and the like, and not say to them, "You are among the people of the Fire, and you will be punished," and things like that which would enrage them and incite them to evil.

As for His saying: "Indeed Satan sows discord among them" [17:53], it is a parenthetical clause: that is, he casts corruption between them and incites some of them against others, so that enmity and strife occur among them.

"And We have not sent you as a guardian over them" [17:54]: that is, not a lord to whom their affairs are entrusted, that you should compel them to Islam and force them to it. Rather, We sent you only as a bringer of good news and a warner. So be lenient with them, and order your companions to show leniency, forbearance, and to avoid contention and confrontation. This was before the revelation of the verse of the sword.

It is also said: it was revealed concerning ʿUmar (may Allah be pleased with him): a man insulted him, and Allah commanded him to pardon. It is also said: the harm the polytheists inflicted on the Muslims became excessive, so they complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and this was revealed. It is also said: "the word that is best" is that they should say, "May Allah guide you, may Allah have mercy on you."

Ṭalḥa recited "yanzaghu" with a kasra (yanzighu). The two are dialectal variants, like yaʿrishūna and yaʿrishūna (both forms of the same verb, differing only in vowel).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 55:

It is a rebuttal of the people of Makkah in their denial and their disbelief that the orphan of Abu Talib should be a prophet, and that the destitute, hungry ones among his companions, such as Suhayb, Bilal, Khabbab and others, should be his followers, rather than that this should be the case with some of their notables and chieftains. That is, "Your Lord knows best who is in the heavens and the earth, and their conditions, their destinies, and what each one of them deserves." As for His saying, ﴿And We have certainly favoured some of the prophets over others﴾, it is an allusion to the preference of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). And His saying, ﴿and We gave David the Zabur﴾, is an indication of the aspect of his preference, namely that he is the Seal of the Prophets and that his community is the best of communities, because that is written in the Zabur of David. Allah the Exalted said, ﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur, after the reminder, that the earth will be inherited by My righteous servants﴾, and they are Muhammad and his community.

If you say: Why did he not define the Zabur (i.e., with the article) as he did in His saying, ﴿And We have certainly written in the Zabur﴾? I say: It is permissible that "Zabur" and "zabur" be like "al-Abbas" and "Abbas", and "al-Fadl" and "Fadl"; and that he intends: "We gave David some of the scriptures (zubur), which are books"; and that he intends what is mentioned in it of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) from the Zabur, and so he named that "Zabur", because it is a part of the Zabur, just as some of the Qur'an is called "Qur'an".

They are the angels. It is also said: Jesus son of Mary, and Ezra (ʿUzayr). And it is said: a group of jinn, whom some people of the Arabs worshipped, and then the jinn embraced Islam without the worshippers realizing it. That is, call upon them, for they cannot remove from you the harm, whether it be sickness, poverty or punishment, nor can they transfer it from one person to another or change it.

﴿Those whom they call upon themselves seek the means of access to their Lord﴾ — Ulāʾika is the subject (mubtadaʾ), alladhīna yadʿūna is its attribute (ṣifa), and yabtaghūna is its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: those gods of theirs seek the means (al-wasīla), which is nearness to Allah, the Exalted.

Ayyuhum is a substitute (badal) for the wāw in yabtaghūna, and ayy is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). That is: they seek whoever among them is nearer and more favoured to Allah as a means, so how much more so one who is not nearer. Or, yabtaghūna al-wasīla is taken to include the sense of yaḥrişūna (they eagerly strive), as if it were said: they eagerly strive to see which of them will be nearer to Allah, and that is through obedience and increasing in goodness and righteousness, and they hope and fear, just as others among the servants of Allah do. So how can they claim that they are gods?

﴿Indeed, the punishment of your Lord is something to be feared﴾ — it is deserving that every person be wary of it, from a nearest angel and a sent prophet, let alone others.

We will destroy them through death and total annihilation, or We will punish them with killing and various kinds of torment. It has also been said: destruction is for the righteous town, and punishment is for the wicked town. And it is related from Muqatil: "I found in the books of al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, in his tafsir of it: As for Mecca, the Abyssinians will ruin it; Medina will be destroyed by hunger; Basra by drowning; Kufa by the Turks; and the mountains by thunderbolts and earthquakes. As for Khurasan, its punishments are of many kinds." Then he mentioned the towns one by one. ﴿In the Book﴾ means in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 59:

The withholding (al-man') is used metaphorically for not sending the signs, on account of the diverting factor of wisdom (ṣārif al-ḥikmah). The first "an" (أن) is in the accusative and the second is in the nominative; its estimated form is: "And what prevented Us from sending the signs was only the denial of the earlier peoples." The intended meaning of "the signs" is those that the Quraysh proposed: turning al-Ṣafā into gold, reviving the dead, and other things. The custom of God regarding nations is that whoever among them proposes a sign, and is granted it, and then does not believe, is feared to be hastened with the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhāb al-istiʾṣāl). So the meaning is: "What diverted Us from sending what they propose of signs was only that those like them, from among those whose hearts were sealed, such as ʿĀd and Thamūd, denied them. And if they were sent, they would have denied them as those had denied, and said, 'This is manifest magic,' as they say regarding other things, and they would have deserved the annihilating punishment. We have resolved to delay the affair of those to whom you were sent until the Day of Resurrection."

Then he mentioned one of those signs, which the earlier peoples had proposed, then denied when they were sent, and so were destroyed: it is the she-camel of Ṣāliḥ, because the traces of their destruction in the land of the Arabs are near their borders, visible to those who travel out and come back. "A clear sign" (mubṣiratan bayyinah). It is also read "mubṣiratan" with a fatḥah on the mīm.

"But they wronged her" (fa-ẓalamū bihā): they disbelieved in her.

"And We send not the signs" (wa-mā nursilu bil-āyāti): if by it is meant the proposed signs, then the meaning is: "We send them not except as a warning (takhwīfan) of the hastened punishment, like a vanguard and forerunner of it; so if they do not fear, it befalls them." If by it is meant other than these, then the meaning is: "And We send what We send of signs, such as the verses of the Qur'an and others, only as a warning (takhwīfan) and admonition (indhāran) of the punishment of the Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 60:

﴿And [remember] when We said to you: Indeed your Lord has encompassed the people.﴾ "And remember when We revealed to you that your Lord has encompassed Quraysh," meaning: We gave you good news of the battle of Badr and of victory over them. This is His saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs﴾ and ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: You will be overcome and gathered [to Hell]﴾ and other such verses. He made it as though it had already happened and been realized, so He said: "He has encompassed the people," in accordance with His habit in reporting [future events]. When the two groups closed in ranks on the day of Badr, the Prophet ﷺ was in the pavilion with Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), supplicating and saying: "O Allah, I ask You for Your covenant and Your promise." Then he went out wearing his armour, urging the people on and saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs.﴾ [[I have not found it in this form. As for its beginning, it is in al-Bukhari, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said while in his tent on the day of Badr: "O Allah, I beseech You for Your covenant and Your promise. O Allah, I beseech You for Your covenant and Your promise. O Allah, if this band perishes, You will not be worshipped after today." Then Abu Bakr took his hand and said: "Enough of that." He went out saying: ﴿The multitude will be routed and they will turn their backs.﴾]] Perhaps Allah, exalted is He, showed him their places of death in his dream, for he used to say when he reached the water of Badr: "By Allah, it is as though I am looking at the places where the people will fall." [[Muslim related it from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "This is the place where so-and-so will fall," and he placed his hand on the ground here. He said: "No one moved from the place where his hand was placed."]] He was pointing to the ground and saying: "This is the place where so-and-so will fall, this is the place where so-and-so will fall." Quraysh heard of what had been revealed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ concerning the matter of the day of Badr and of what he had been shown in his dream of their places of death, so they would laugh, mock, and hasten [the matter] in derision. **Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 17, verses 61–65**

*Tina* (clay) is a circumstantial accusative (*hal*, a noun in the accusative that describes the state of another noun at the time of an action). It may refer back to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*), with *asjudu* (prostrate) as its governing verb, so the sense is: "Shall I prostrate myself to him when he is clay?", meaning that his origin is clay.

Or it may refer to the pronoun returning from the relative clause, so the sense is: "Shall I prostrate myself to one who, at the time of his creation, was clay?"

﴿Have You seen this one whom You have honored above me?﴾ The *ka* (*ka*-, "you") is the address particle, and *hadha* (this) is its object. The meaning is: "Tell me about this one whom You have honored over me, that is, whom You have preferred. Why did You honor him over me when I am better than him?" The speech is abbreviated by omitting this, and then he begins: ﴿If You give me respite until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except for a few.﴾ The *lam* (*la-*) is an introductory particle (*lam al-muwatta'ah*) preceding the omitted oath, and *la-ahtanikanna* means "I will surely uproot them with misguidance." It derives from *ihtanaka al-jarad al-ard*, which means that the locust consumed everything on the land, and it comes from the word *hanak* (jaw). From this comes what Sibawayh mentioned: *ahnaka al-shatin*, meaning he ate both of them.

If it is asked: "From where did he know that this would be easy for him, when it is unseen?" The answer is either that he heard it from the angels, to whom God had announced it; or that he derived it from their statement, ﴿Will You place in it one who causes corruption therein?﴾; or that he looked at him and perceived from his signs that he had a lustful nature. It has been said that he said this when he knew his whispering would reach Adam.

Apparently he said this before Adam ate from the tree.

﴿Go﴾ (*idhhab*) is not from *dhahab* (going), which is the opposite of coming. Its meaning is: "Proceed to your affair which you have chosen, through abandonment and leaving you alone." He follows this with a mention of what his bad choice brought upon him in the words: ﴿As for whoever follows you among them, indeed Hell is your recompense, a full recompense.﴾ This is like what Moses, peace be upon him, said to the Samiri: ﴿Go, for you have in life [the saying] "No touching."﴾

If it is asked: "Should the pronoun in *jaza'* (recompense) not be in the third person, to refer back to *man tabi'aka* (whoever follows you)?" The answer is: Yes, but the intended meaning is: "Indeed Hell is their recompense and yours," and then the addressed (second person) prevailed over the absent (third person), so it is said *jaza'ukum* (your recompense). It is also permissible that it refers to the followers, by way of *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person within a discourse).

*Jaza'an mawfuran* (a full recompense) is in the accusative because of the meaning of "you will be repaid" implied in ﴿indeed Hell is your recompense﴾, or because of an implied verb "you will be repaid," or as a circumstantial accusative, since the recompense is described as *mawfur* (full), and *al-mawfur* means *al-muwaffar* (the fully given). It is said: *farra lisahibika 'irdah* (he gave his companion his honour in full).

*Istafazzahu* means he made him light-headed (*istakhaffahu*). *Al-fazz* is the light one. *Wa-ajlib* (and urge) derives from *al-jalabah*, which is shouting (the printed text reads "*al-sabah*," but the lexicon has "*al-sayah*" [shouting]). *Al-khayl* refers to cavalry.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "O cavalry of God, mount up!" [Abu al-Shaykh reported it in *al-Nasikh wal-Mansukh* through the chain of Abu Hamzah al-Sukkari, from Abd al-Karim, who said: Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated to me the story of the people who waged war. He said: "Some people came to the Prophet ﷺ and said: 'We pledge allegiance to you for Islam,'" and he mentioned the story, in which the Prophet ﷺ commanded that it be announced among the people: "O cavalry of God, mount up!" So they mounted, and no horseman waited for another horseman. Ibn A'idh reported in *al-Maghazi* from al-Walid ibn Muslim, from Sa'id ibn Bashir, from Qatadah, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ sent (on the day of Quraydhah, the day of the Confederates) a crier who called: "O cavalry of God, mount up!" Al-Suhayli, in *al-Rawd*, attributed this expression in the battle of Hunayn to Sahih Muslim, and it should be examined there. Abu Dawud said in *al-Sunan*: "Chapter: the call at the time of alarm: 'O cavalry of God, mount up!'" and he cited in the chapter the hadith of Samurah ibn Jundub, that the Prophet ﷺ named our horses "the horses of God." I say: This was difficult for the one who investigates the source of the hadith, and he said: "It is open to question for one who considers it." It seems that the correspondence between the hadith and the chapter title did not become clear to him, though it is evident, because the intended point is the validity of this attribution. It is also reported from Ali and Khalid ibn al-Walid. In *al-Mustadrak* of al-Hakim, in the story of Uways, from the hadith of Abu Nadrah, from Usayd ibn Jabir, he mentioned the story, and at its end: "Ali called out: 'O cavalry of God, mount up!'" In *al-Riddah* by al-Waqidi, from the narration of Asim ibn Umar, from Mahmud ibn Labid, Khalid ibn al-Walid said to his companions on the day of Yamamah: "O cavalry of God, mount up!" So they mounted and marched against the Banu Hanifah.]

*Al-rajl* is a collective noun for *al-rajil* (foot soldier). Its parallel is *al-rakb* (riders) and *al-sahb* (companions). It is recited as *wa-rajlika* (and your foot soldiers), on the basis that *fa'l* means *fa'il*, as in *ta'iba* and *ta'ib* (weary). Its meaning is: "And gather your foot soldiers." Its *jim* may also be vowelled with *damm* (u), so it would be like *hadath* and *hudath*, and *nadas* and *nudas*, and their similar forms.

It is said: *rajul* and *rajul* (both forms of the same word). It is also recited as *wa-rijalika* and *wa-rijalika* (and your men).

If it is asked: "What is the meaning of Iblis's inciting by his voice and his urging by his cavalry and foot soldiers?" The answer is: This is a statement that came in the manner of a parable. His state, in his domination over the one he misleads, is depicted as a fierce warrior who fell upon a people, shouted at them with a cry that stirred them from their places and disturbed them from their positions, and urged his army of horsemen and foot soldiers against them until he uprooted them. It has been said: "By his voice" means by his calling to evil. "His cavalry and foot soldiers" means:

"Every rider and walker from among the people of corruption."

[*Al-ʿayth* in *al-Sihah* means corruption.]

It has been said: It is permissible that Iblis has cavalry and foot soldiers. As for sharing in wealth and children, it refers to every disobedience to which he drives them in these two domains, such as usury, unlawful earnings, the *bahirah* and *sa'ibah* (pagan practices), spending in immorality, extravagance, withholding the zakat, seeking children by unlawful means, claiming a child without cause, naming them *Abd al-'Uzza* and *Abd al-Harith* (servant of al-'Uzza, servant of al-Harith), Judaizing and Christianizing them, pushing them toward blameworthy crafts and forbidden acts, and other things.

﴿And promise them﴾ means false promises: intercession by idols, honour before God through noble lineages, postponing repentance, forgiveness of sins without it, reliance upon mercy, and the intercession of the Messenger in major sins and the removal from the Fire after they have become charred cinders. [*Hummam* in *al-Sihah* are ashes and charcoal, the singular being *hummah*.] Also preferring the immediate to the deferred.

[Commentary of Ibn al-Munayyir (Ahmad): Here the author (al-Zamakhshari) follows the Sunnah and those who follow it, for he counted the forgiveness connected with God's will, even if it were not repentance for believers, among the promises of Satan, while it is known that it is established by definitive Qur'anic texts as a promise from the Merciful. Likewise the intercession agreed upon among the People of the Sunnah and the Community, with which the truthful and believed one (the Prophet ﷺ) was promised, and by which God distinguished him over every creature, is among the vain promises of Satan and his baseless wishes. O God, grant us intercession, and gather us in the company of the Sunnah and the Community.]

[The phrase "after they have become charred cinders" in *al-Sihah*: *al-hummam* are ashes and charcoal, and *hummah* is one piece. Then, what he states about forgiveness depending on repentance, and the absence of intercession for major sins, and the non-exit of their people from the Fire after they are burned, is the doctrine of the Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school holding that the grave sinner is in an intermediate state and that forgiveness requires repentance). The People of the Sunnah hold otherwise, as established in the science of tawhid (theology). (ʿ)]

﴿Indeed, My servants, over them you have no authority﴾ means: you cannot mislead them. ﴿And your Lord suffices as a Guardian﴾ for them, in whom they trust, seeking refuge in Him from you. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿except Your sincere servants among them.﴾

If it is asked: "How was it permissible for God to command Iblis to have power over His servants, leading them astray, calling them to evil, and turning them away from good?" The answer is: This is among the commands that came by way of abandonment and leaving alone, as He said to the disobedient: "Do whatever you wish."

It may refer back to the relative pronoun (*al-mawsul*), with *asjudu* (prostrate) as its governing verb, so the sense is: "Shall I prostrate myself to him when he is clay?", meaning that his origin is clay.

That feeling of security led you to turn away. If you ask, "What is ﴿جانِبَ الْبَرِّ﴾ governed by?" the answer is that it is the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *yakhsifa*, like ﴿الْأَرْضَ﴾ in the phrase ﴿فَخَسَفْنا بِهِ وَبِدارِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾, "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home." ﴿وَبِكُمْ﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). The meaning is: "that He may cause the side of the land to swallow, that is, overturn it, while you are upon it."

If you ask, "What is the point of mentioning the side?" the answer is that all sides and directions are equal in His power. In every direction, whether land or sea, He has a watchful cause of destruction. The side of the sea is not alone in this. If drowning happens on the sea side, the land side has its equivalent, which is being swallowed, since it is concealment under the earth just as drowning is concealment under the water. Land and sea are alike to Him: He has power on land as He has power on the sea. So the intelligent person should make his fear of God equal in all directions and every place.

﴿أَوْ يُرْسِلَ عَلَيْكُمْ حاصِباً﴾ means a wind that pelts with pebbles (*ḥaṣbā'*), that is, it throws them. The meaning is: "Or if He does not strike you with destruction from beneath you through being swallowed, He will strike you with it from above you through a wind He sends against you, carrying pebbles with which He stones you. This will be more severe for you than drowning in the sea." ﴿وَكِيلًا﴾ means one who will take charge of averting that from you.

﴿أَمْ أَمِنْتُمْ﴾ means: "Or do you feel secure that He will strengthen your motives and supply your needs until you return and board the sea from which He saved you, and so you turn away? Then He will take vengeance on you by sending against you ﴿قاصِفاً﴾, a wind that has a *qaṣīf*, which is a violent sound, as if it breaks things (*tatqaṣṣafu*), that is, shatters them." It is said: it is the wind that does not pass over anything without breaking it. ﴿فَيُغْرِقَكُمْ﴾ is also read with the *tā'* (feminine form, referring to the wind), and with the *nūn*. The same applies to ﴿نَخْسِفَ﴾, ﴿نُرْسِلَ﴾, and ﴿نُعِيدَكُمْ﴾.

﴿التَّبِيعُ﴾ is read with *yā'* and with *nūn*. *Al-tabī'* means the one who pursues demands, from the phrase ﴿فَاتِّباعٌ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ﴾, "then pursuit according to what is fair," meaning a demand. Al-Shammākh said:

"Just as the debtor takes refuge from the pursuing creditor."

The poet describes an eagle from which foxes of the two eastern regions flee. The "two eastern regions" is either a place-name, or the south and north directions, like "the two easts." *Lāda* means fled and sought refuge. *Al-gharīm* means the debtor. *Min al-tabī'* means from the creditor who demands repayment.

It is said: "So-and-so has a *tabī'* over so-and-so," meaning he has control over him and demands his right. The meaning is: "We do what We do to them, and then you will find no one who pursues Us for what We have done, seeking retribution or to avenge on Our behalf." This is like His saying ﴿وَلا يَخافُ عُقْباها﴾, "and He does not fear its consequence."

﴿بِما كَفَرْتُمْ﴾ means: by your ingratitude for the blessing, meaning their turning away when He had saved them.

The hamza in ﴿أَفَأَمِنْتُمْ﴾ is the interrogative hamza of denial (*hamzat al-inkar*), and the fa' coordinates with an elided clause whose sense is: "Were you saved, and so you felt secure?" That feeling of security led you to turn away. If you ask, "What is ﴿جانِبَ الْبَرِّ﴾ governed by?" the answer is that it is the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*) of *yakhsifa*, like ﴿الْأَرْضَ﴾ in the phrase ﴿فَخَسَفْنا بِهِ وَبِدارِهِ الْأَرْضَ﴾, "So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home." ﴿وَبِكُمْ﴾ is a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*). The meaning is: "that He may cause the side of the land to swallow, that is, overturn it, while you are upon it."

If you ask, "What is the point of mentioning the side?" the answer is that all sides and directions are equal in His power. In every direction, whether land or sea, He has a watchful cause of destruction. The side of the sea is not alone in this.
