Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 70:

It has been said, regarding the honouring of the children of Adam: Allah honoured him with reason, speech, discernment, writing, a beautiful form, an upright stature, and the management of his livelihood and his final return. It has also been said that it is by giving them dominion over what is on the earth and subjecting it to them.

It has been said: every creature eats with its mouth except the son of Adam. And it is reported from al-Rashid that he had food brought and asked for spoons, while Abu Yusuf was present. He said to him: "It has come in the commentary of your grandfather Ibn Abbas on the words of the Exalted, ﴿And We have honoured the children of Adam﴾, that He made for them fingers with which to eat." So spoons were brought, and he pushed them away and ate with his fingers. ﴿And preferred them above many of those We have created﴾ means above all besides the angels.

[[Mahmud said: "The meaning is that We preferred them over all other than the angels... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "He has reached a level of foolishness that requires the prescribed punishment, and we are only contending with him on the basis of knowledge, not on the basis of his foolishness. The aspect specific to this verse is that taking 'many' to mean 'all' is neither unlikely nor objectionable. Do you not see that the use of the lesser to mean none is attested? Al-Zamakhshari favours this in the Exalted's words ﴿So little do they believe﴾ and similar instances are numerous. The poet alluded to this in his saying:

'Few are the voices in it except its bleating,'

meaning there are no voices in it. We may leave it as it is and say: created beings are of two kinds, the children of Adam being one kind, and all other created beings the other kind. Without doubt, the others are more numerous than them, even if they were not much more numerous. So the meaning of His words ﴿and preferred them above many of those We have created﴾ is: above others, of all created beings. Those others are many without dispute. This is equivalent to your saying: 'and We preferred them above all others among those We created.' The apparent meaning of the verse is therefore with the Ash'arites, whom he named 'Mujbira' (determinists), and he was extravagant in reviling them and produced ornate phrases in deriding them. 'Not a word does he utter but there is a watcher by him, ready.' And Allah is the Guardian of success and right guidance."]] It is enough of an honour for the children of Adam that the angels are raised above them, when they are what they are, and their rank with Allah is their rank.

How strange it is that the Mujbira (Jabriyya) reversed matters in everything and contradicted the evidence! Stubbornness drove them to the great error of preferring a human over an angel. This happened after they heard Allah's exalting of their affair and His multiplying of them, together with His honouring of their mention, and they knew where He settled them, how He brought them near, and how He placed them with respect to His prophets as the prophets' place is with respect to their communities. Then excessive partisanship drove them to fabricate sayings and reports, among them: "The angels said: 'Our Lord, You have given the children of Adam this world, to eat from it and enjoy it, and You have not given us that; so give us it in the next world.' He said: 'By My might and My majesty, I will not make the offspring of those whom I created with My hand like those to whom I said: "Be," and it was.'" [[His words "The angels said: 'Our Lord, You have given the children of Adam this world'" begin, as in al-Khazin: "When Allah created Adam and his offspring, the angels said..." and his words "created with My hand" in al-Khazin: "and I breathed into him of My spirit." (Gh.)]]

[[It was narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, from the route of Muhammad ibn Mahan, from Talha ibn Zayd, from Safwan ibn Sulaym, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Abdullah ibn Umar, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The angels said: 'Lord, You have given the children of Adam the world, to eat in it, drink, and wear clothes; and we glorify Your praise, we do not eat, drink, or amuse ourselves. Just as You gave them the world, give us the Hereafter.' He said: 'I will not make the offspring of those I created with My hand like those to whom I said: "Be," and it was.'" He said: "Only Talha and Abu Ghassan narrated it from Safwan, and Talha ibn Muhammad ibn Mahan alone transmitted it. Its route through Abu Ghassan Hajjaj al-A'war was recorded by al-Tabarani in al-Mu'jam al-Kabir, and its narrators are trustworthy." It has a witness in the tafsir of Abd al-Razzaq, from Ma'mar, from Zayd ibn Aslam, who said: "The angels said," and mentioned something similar, as a statement of his own. Al-Daraqutni said in al-'Ilal: "Abd al-Majid ibn Abi Dawud narrated it from Ma'mar, from Zayd ibn Aslam, from Ata' ibn Yasar, from Ibn Umar," and he mentioned something similar. He said: "Shurayh ibn Yunus narrated it from Abd al-Majid as a statement of Ibn Umar, and this is more sound." It has another witness, recorded by al-Tabarani in Musnad al-Shamiyyin and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat, from the narration of Abd Rabbih ibn Salih, from Urwa ibn Ruwayh, that he heard him narrate from Jabir, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When Allah created Adam and his offspring, the angels said: 'O Lord, You created them to eat, drink, marry, and ride; so give them the world and give us the Hereafter.' He, exalted, said: 'I will not make those I created with My hand like those to whom I said: "Be," and it was.'" Among them is what he narrated from Abu Hurayra, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "A believer is more honoured by Allah than the angels who are with Him." Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated it through Hammad ibn Salama, from Abu al-Mihzam, from Abu Hurayra, as a statement of his own, and Ibn Majah recorded it through this route as his statement. Abu al-Mihzam is abandoned (matruk). It has a witness recorded by al-Tabarani and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab, through the narration of Ubayd Allah ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Nothing is more honoured by Allah on the Day of Resurrection than the children of Adam." It was said: "Nor the angels?" He said: "Nor the angels. The angels are compelled, like the sun and the moon." Al-Bayhaqi said: "Ubayd Allah ibn Tammam alone transmitted it; he narrates the hadiths of Mu'awiya, and he is weak."]] And they narrated from Abu Hurayra that he said: "A believer [[His words "He said: 'A believer is more honoured by me than the angels'" in al-Khazin: "the believer." (Gh.)]] is more honoured by Allah than the angels who are with Him."

Among their audacities is that they interpreted "many" in this verse to mean "all," and they were abandoned by God, until they lost their sense of taste and did not feel the ugliness of their statement: "And We preferred them above all of those We created." Yet the meaning of their phrase "above all of those We created" is more distressing to their throats and more irritating to their eyes, but they do not perceive it. Look at their contrivances and their clinging to remote interpretations out of enmity toward the Exalted Assembly, as though Gabriel, peace be upon him, had angered them when he destroyed the cities of the people of Lut. That rancour does not dissolve from their hearts. [[His words "That rancour does not dissolve from their hearts": in al-Sihah, "al-sakhima" is resentment and grudge in the soul. (Gh.)]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 71:

It is recited as "yad'ū" with the yā' and the nūn (i.e., "nad'ū"). And "yud'ā kull unās" is recited with the passive form. Al-Hasan recited "yad'wā kull unās," with the alif changed to a wāw, in the dialect of those who say "ifw^a" (for "ifā," "call/come"). The adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is in the accusative, governed by an implied "udhkur" (remember).

It is permissible to say that the nūn is the sign of the plural, as in ﴿وَأَسَرُّوا النَّجْوَى الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ ("and they secretly conferred, those who did wrong"), and the nominative is implied, as in "yud'ā" (the verb being passive), and the nūn was not written out, out of indifference toward it, since it is not a pronoun but merely a sign.

﴿بِإِمامِهِمْ﴾ means: with those whom they followed, whether a prophet, a leader in religion, a book, or a religion [[Maḥmūd said: "'With their imam' means with whom they followed, from a prophet or a book or a religion... etc." Aḥmad said: He has indeed invented a novelty in both wording and meaning, for the known plural of umm is ummahāt. As for honouring ʿĪsā (peace be upon him) by mentioning the mothers of all creation so that he may be recalled through his mother, this implies that the creation of ʿĪsā without a father is a flaw in his station, whereas the reverse is the truth: his creation without a father was a sign for him and a mark of honour concerning him. And God knows best.]], so it is said: "O followers of so-and-so, O people of such-and-such a religion and such-and-such a book." It was also said: "with the book of their deeds," so it is said: "O companions of the book of good, and O companions of the book of evil." In the recitation of al-Hasan: "with their book." Among the strange interpretations is that the word "imam" is the plural of "umm" (mother), that people will be called on the Day of Resurrection by their mothers, and that the wisdom in calling by mothers rather than fathers is to honour the right of ʿĪsā (peace be upon him), to display the nobility of al-Ḥasan and al-Ḥusayn, and so that the children of fornication are not disgraced. I would like to know which of these is more novel: the soundness of its wording or the brilliance of its wisdom?

﴿فَمَنْ أُوتِيَ مِنْ هؤُلاءِ الْمَدْعُوِّينَ كِتابَهُ بِيَمِينِهِ فَأُولئِكَ يَقْرَؤُنَ كِتابَهُمْ﴾ ("Whoever among these summoned ones is given his book in his right hand, those will read their book"). It was said "ulā'ika" (those) because "man" (whoever) carries the meaning of the plural.

If you say: why were the companions of the right hand singled out for reading their book, as though the companions of the left do not read their book? I say: Yes, but when they are made aware of what is in their book, what seizes them is what seizes one who is confronted with his offences and made to acknowledge his evils, namely shame, embarrassment, abasement, a stammering tongue, faltering, inability to form the words of speech, and losing the ability to order one's speech. Thus their reading is as though it were no reading at all. As for the companions of the right hand, their situation is the opposite of this: they will undoubtedly read their book in the best and clearest manner, and they will not be satisfied with reading it alone, until the reader says to the people of the gathering: ﴿هَاؤُمُ اقْرَؤُا كِتابِيَهْ﴾ ("Here, read my book!") ﴿وَلا يُظْلَمُونَ فَتِيلاً﴾ ("and they will not be wronged even a thread"), and they will not have the least thing reduced from their reward, like His saying ﴿وَلا يُظْلَمُونَ شَيْئاً﴾ ("and they will not be wronged in the least"), ﴿فَلا يَخافُ ظُلْماً وَلا هَضْماً﴾ ("so he will fear no wrong nor any diminishing").

Its meaning: whoever is blind in this world will be blind in the Hereafter as well, and even more astray in the way (wa-aḍalla sabīlan). The word "blind" (a'mā) is used figuratively for one whose faculty of sight is corrupted and who cannot perceive visible things; it applies to one who is not guided to the path of salvation. In this world it is because of the loss of sight; in the Hereafter it is because guidance to it will not benefit him. They have also permitted that the second (a'mā in wa-aḍalla) be in the sense of the comparative (tafḍīl) [[He returned to his speech. He said: "They have also permitted that the second be in the sense of the comparative... etc." Aḥmad says: that is, because it is from blindness of the heart, not blindness of the eye, so it is permissible for the form afʿal to be derived from it.]]. For this reason Abū ʿAmr read the first (a'mā) with imāla (inclination of the alif) and the second with tafkhīm (emphatic pronunciation), because the comparative form (afʿal al-tafḍīl) is completed by min (than), so its alif is in the position of one standing in the middle of the utterance [[His words "standing in the middle of the utterance" is perhaps "the word," as in the expression of al-Nasafi. (ʿ)]], as in your saying: aʿmālukum (your deeds). As for the first, nothing is attached to it, so its alif stands at the end, open to imāla.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 73–75:

It is related that the tribe of Thaqif said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We will not enter into your affair unless you grant us privileges by which we may boast over the Arabs: we shall not pay the ʿushr (tithe), nor be mobilised (for the ḥashr, levy of troops), nor perform the tajbiya [[His saying "we shall not pay the ʿushr, nor be mobilised, nor perform the tajbiya" — in the Ṣiḥāḥ, the tajbiya (a technical term meaning a rite of bowing) is that a person stands in the posture of one bowing in ruku'. Abu ʿUbayda said: it occurs in two states: one, that one places one's hands on one's knees; and the other, that one prostrates oneself on one's face kneeling, which is the sujūd. And in it (the Ṣiḥāḥ) is "Wajj", the name of the town of al-Ṭāʾif. Also in it: "ʿaḍadtu al-shajar", meaning I cut the tree. (ʿ)]] in our prayer; every usury (ribā) owed to us is ours, and every usury owed by us is remitted from us; you must allow us to enjoy al-Lāt for a year, and we will not break it with our own hands at the end of the year; and you must forbid anyone from entering our valley of Wajj, and cutting its trees. If the Arabs ask you, 'Why have you done this?', say: 'God has commanded me to do it.'" They brought their document, and it was written: "In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Compassionate. This is a document from Muhammad, the Messenger of God, to Thaqif:

They shall not pay the ʿushr, nor be mobilised." They said: "Nor shall they perform the tajbiya." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) remained silent. Then they said to the scribe: "Write: nor shall they perform the tajbiya." The scribe was looking at the Messenger of God. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him) stood up, drew his sword and said: "O assembly of Thaqif, you have inflamed the heart of our Prophet — may God inflame your hearts with fire!" They said: "We were not speaking to you, but to Muhammad." So this verse was revealed. [[I have not found it. al-Thaʿlabi mentioned it from Ibn ʿAbbas without a chain.]]

It is also related that the Quraysh said to him: "Make a sign of mercy into a sign of punishment, and a sign of punishment into a sign of mercy, so that we may believe in you." So this was revealed: ﴿And they had almost tempted you away from that which We have revealed to you, that you should fabricate against Us other than it; and then they would have taken you as a friend.﴾ The particle "in" (wa-in) here is the lightened form of the heavy (in), and the lām is what distinguishes it from the negating particle. The meaning: the matter is that they nearly tempted you, i.e., deceived you, enticing you away from ﴿that which We have revealed to you﴾ of Our commands, Our prohibitions, Our promise and Our threat, ﴿that you should fabricate against Us﴾, that you should say about Us what We have not said — meaning what they wanted of you: the changing of promise into threat and threat into promise, and what Thaqif proposed, that you should attribute to God what He had not sent down to you. ﴿And then they would have taken you as a friend﴾, i.e., had you followed their wishes, they would have taken you as a friend, and you would have been their ally and would have left My guardianship. ﴿And had We not made you firm﴾, had it not been for Our making you steadfast and Our protecting you, ﴿you would nearly have inclined toward them a little﴾, you would have nearly leaned towards their deception and their guile. This is an incitement from God to him and a favour of steadfastness, and in it is a kindness to the believers. ﴿Then We would have made you taste a double portion of life and a double portion of death﴾ — i.e., We would have made you taste the punishment of the Hereafter and the punishment of the grave, doubled. If you say: what is the real nature of this speech? I say: its origin is "We would have made you taste the punishment of life and the punishment of death", because punishment is of two kinds: punishment in death, which is the punishment of the grave, and punishment in the life of the Hereafter, which is the punishment of the Fire. And "ḍiʿf" (double, multiple) may be predicated of it, as in His saying ﴿so give them a double punishment from the Fire﴾, meaning doubled. So the original sentence was: "We would have made you taste a double punishment in life and a double punishment in death." [[Maḥmūd said: "The intended meaning is the double of the punishment of life and the double of the punishment of death ... etc." Aḥmad said: As for diminishing the near-inclination, what should be taken as its meaning is that it is an occurrence in God's knowledge, the Mighty and Majestic, for God knows what has not happened, had it happened how it would have happened. So He, exalted, knew that the inclining that nearly took place from him, peace be upon him, though what happened was a small matter and a slight thing, is a report from God, exalted, about what is in His knowledge as a estimate; so it is not fitting to take it as exaggeration and warning, for that would not occur in reports. Do you not see that if the actual occurrence had been a great inclination, its diminishing would have been a failing in the report; and it is not denied that a sin grows greater according to its doer, as is reported: "the good deeds of the righteous are the bad deeds of those brought near." As for Zamakhshari's transmission from his shaykhs of their magnifying the attribution of abominations and ugly things to God, the Mighty and Majestic — they magnified a great thing which it is incumbent upon every Muslim to find dreadful; but they were ignorant that believing ugliness to be an essential attribute of the ugly leads them to conclude that every act deemed ugly in a servant is deemed ugly in God, which is an error on their part. The meaning of an act being ugly is that God, exalted, has forbidden it to His servant, even though it is permissible for God to do it, and it is good with respect to Him: "He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned" [Q. 21:23]. Do you not see that a king may rightly find it ugly that his servant sit on his throne, and forbid him from it, yet he does not find it ugly for himself; rather it is good and beautiful for him. And his shaykhs were occupied with magnifying what they were bound to of association, away from magnifying what is other than it, which is pure monotheism and sheer faith; but their own bad belief adorned for them, so they saw it as good. And God is the Granter of success.]]. Then the qualifier was deleted and the attribute put in its place, namely "double" (ḍiʿf). Then the attribute was made the annexed term in the manner of the qualified noun, so one says "ḍiʿf al-ḥayā and ḍiʿf al-mamāt", just as if one said: "We would have made you taste painful life and painful death." It is also permissible that by "double of life" is meant: the punishment of the present life, and by "double of death": what follows death, of the punishment of the grave and the punishment of the Fire. The meaning: We would have doubled for you the punishment hastened upon the disobedient in the present world, and what We delay until after death.

In the mention of the near-inclination and its diminution, together with the following of it by a severe threat of doubled punishment in both abodes, there is clear evidence that the ugliness of an act grows according to the greatness of the standing and elevated rank of its doer. For this reason the shaykhs of justice and monotheism [[His saying "the shaykhs of justice" means the Muʿtazila. By "the compellers" (al-mujbira) he means the people of the Sunna, who said that good and evil both come from God by His creating and willing them, even if they are apparently the act of the servant. (ʿ)]] — may God be pleased with them — declined to attribute ugliness to God, exalted be He far above that. And in it is evidence that the slightest flattery of the deviators is opposed to God, a departure from His guardianship, and a cause that calls for His anger and His punishment.

So upon the believer, when he recites this verse, is that he should kneel at it and reflect upon it, for it is worthy of reflection, and the one who looks into it should feel awe and an increase in firmness in the religion of God. Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 76–77:

﴿And indeed they were about to unsettle you (yastafizzunaka)﴾ from the land: that is, the people of Makkah were about to drive you out through their enmity and their scheming, from the land of Makkah. ﴿And then they would not remain (la yalbathun)﴾ after your expulsion ﴿except for a little time﴾. ﴿Surely God will destroy them﴾, and it happened as He said, for they were destroyed at Badr shortly after his expulsion. It has also been said that the meaning is: even if they had expelled you, they would have been utterly uprooted, every one of them. But they did not expel him; rather, he emigrated by the command of his Lord.

It has been said that it means "from the land of the Arabs." It has also been said that it means "from the land of Madinah." This is because when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) emigrated, the Jews envied him and disliked his nearness to them. So they gathered around him and said: "O Abu al-Qasim, the prophets were sent only to al-Sham, which is a sacred land and was the place of emigration of Ibrahim. If you went out to al-Sham, we would believe in you and follow you. We know that nothing prevents you from leaving except fear of the Byzantines (al-Rum). So if you are the Messenger of God, then God will protect you from them." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then mobilised his army at a distance of miles from Madinah, and it was said at Dhu al-Hulayfah, so that his companions would gather to him and people would see him determined to march to al-Sham, out of his eagerness for people to enter the religion of God. Then the revelation came down, and he turned back.

[[I have not found it. Al-Suhayli mentioned it in al-Rawd, from Abd al-Majid ibn Bahram ibn Shihr ibn Hawshab, from Abd al-Rahman ibn Ghanm: "The Jews came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Abu al-Qasim, if you are truthful, that you are a prophet, then go to al-Sham." He then related something similar, but said: "So he undertook the expedition of Tabuk, intending only al-Sham. When he reached Tabuk, God the Exalted sent down—" and he mentioned it, and added: "And He commanded him to return." And he said: "In it (al-Sham) is your life and your death, and from it you will be raised."]]

It was read as ﴿la yalbathun﴾. In the reading of Ubayy it is ﴿la yalbathu﴾ with the governance of "idha" (the particle "idha," meaning "then" or "in that case," which governs the verb in the subjunctive-like construction). If you ask: what is the basis of the two readings? I answer: as for the widely transmitted reading, the verb has been conjoined to the verb, and it is in the nominative (marfu') because it occurs as the predicate of kada (the verb "to be about to"), and the verb in the predicate of kada takes the place of a noun. As for the reading of Ubayy, it contains a complete clause, which is ﴿idha la yalbathu﴾, conjoined to the clause of his saying ﴿wa in kadu la-yastafizzunaka﴾.

It was read as ﴿khilafaka﴾ (instead of ﴿khalfaka﴾, the reading explained earlier). The poet said:

*"The abodes were effaced after them (khilafahum), as if the palm-weavers had spread a mat between them."*

Effaced: meaning worn away and destroyed. Khilafahum: that is, after them. The shawatib are women who split palm fronds, that is, their green leaves, and make them into mats. The verse describes their dwellings after them by their decay and the abundance of their refuse, due to their not being swept.

That is, after them, ﴿the way of those whom We sent before you﴾. He means that every people who expelled their messenger from among them, God's way is to destroy them. It is accusative (nasb) as an absolute object (masdar mu'akkid), meaning: God has established this as a way.

Ishaq said in his Musnad: Bishr ibn Umar related to us, Sulayman ibn Bilal related to us, Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, Abu Bakr ibn Hazm related to me from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: Stand up and pray. And that was at dulook al-shams, when it leaned. So he stood and prayed the Zuhr, four rak'as. Ibn Mardawayh also related it by this route. And this is munqati' (broken in its chain).]]: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me at the dulook of the sun, when the sun declined, and he led me in the Zuhr prayer." Its derivation is from al-dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eye when he looks at it. So if dulook means the decline (zawal), then the verse encompasses the five prayers; and if it means the setting (ghuroob), then the Zuhr and 'Asr have been excluded from it. Al-Ghasaq: the darkness, and it is the time of the 'Isha' prayer. "Wa Qur'an al-Fajr" (and the recitation of dawn): the Fajr prayer. It was named "Qur'an," which is recitation (al-qira'a), because recitation is a pillar (rukn) of it, just as it was named ruku' (bowing), sujud (prostration) and qunut (devotion). And this is a proof against Ibn 'Ulayya and al-Asamm in their claim that recitation is not a pillar. "Mashhudan" (witnessed): witnessed by the angels of the night and the day; these descend and those ascend, so it is at the end of the night's register and the beginning of the day's register. Or it is witnessed by a large number of worshippers customarily. Or it is due that it be witnessed by a large congregation. It is permissible that "Wa Qur'an al-Fajr" is an exhortation to lengthen the recitation in the Fajr prayer, because it is one in which people are crowded, so that people hear the Qur'an and the reward increases; and for this reason Fajr was the longest of the prayers in recitation. "Wa min al-layli" (and during part of the night): "And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as an extra (nafilah) for you." Tahajjud is abandoning sleep for prayer, and similar to it is ta'ththum (avoiding sin) and taharruj (avoiding wrongdoing). It is also said of sleep: tahajjada. "Nafilah laka": an additional act of worship for you beyond the five prayers. Nafilah was placed in the position of tahajjud, because tahajjud is an additional act of worship, so tahajjud and nafilah share one meaning. The meaning is that tahajjud is an addition for you upon the obligatory prayers, an obligation specific to you alone without others, since it is a voluntary act for them. "Maqaman mahmudan" is in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), meaning: "It may be that your Lord raises you up on the Day of Resurrection and establishes you in a praiseworthy station." Or "yab'athaka" is taken to imply the meaning of "yuqimuka" (establishes you). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: that He raises you possessing a praiseworthy station. The meaning of "al-maqam al-mahmud": the station in which the one standing is praised, and everyone who sees it and recognizes it praises it; it is absolute in every matter deserving praise among kinds of honours. It was also said: the intended meaning is intercession (al-shafa'a), which is one type of what it encompasses. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: a station in which the first and last of creation praise you, and in which you are elevated above all creation: you ask and you are given, you intercede and your intercession is accepted; no one is except under your banner.

From Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): it is the station in which I will intercede for my ummah [[Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tirmidhi related it through Dawud ibn Yazid al-Awdi from his father from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words, "It may be that your Lord raises you up to a praiseworthy station," and he was asked about it, and he said: "It is the intercession." And on this topic, from Anas in al-Bukhari's Tawhid; from Ibn 'Umar in his (al-Bukhari's) Zakat. And from Ibn Mas'ud in al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim, and it has another route in Ahmad and al-Hakim, expanded. And from Ka'b ibn Malik in al-Hakim. Its origin is in Muslim. And from Jabir in Ahmad and al-Hakim, and its connection and disconnection on al-Zuhri from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn is disputed. And from Abu Sa'id in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Maja. And from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather in Ibn Mardawayh, expanded. And from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in Ibn Mardawayh, through the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan from Abu Hanifa from 'Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Rabi' from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the praiseworthy station, and he said: It is the intercession."]]. And from Hudhayfa: Allah gathers the people in one plain, so that no soul speaks, and the first to be called is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he says: "Here I am at Your service, and I am happy to serve You; the evil is not attributed to You; the guided one is the one You have guided; Your servant is before You, by You and toward You; there is no refuge and no escape from You except toward You; You are blessed and exalted, glory be to You, Lord of the House." He said: this is His saying, "It may be that your Lord raises you up to a praiseworthy station" [[al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tabari, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar and Abu Nu'aym in his biography of Hudhayfa in al-Hilya, all through the route of Shu'ba and Isra'il, both from Abu Ishaq, who said: I heard 'Utba ibn Zafar say: I heard Hudhayfa say, "Allah gathers the people," and he mentioned it.]].

Dalakat al-shams: it set (ghaaribat). It was also said: it declined (zaalat). It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) [[Al-Bayhaqi related it through Ayyub ibn Utba from Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm from Urwa from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) when the sun had dalaka - that is, when it had declined - and said: Stand up and pray. So he stood and prayed the Zuhr." Ishaq said in his Musnad: Bishr ibn Umar related to us, Sulayman ibn Bilal related to us, Yahya ibn Sa'id related to us, Abu Bakr ibn Hazm related to me from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: Jibril came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said to him: Stand up and pray. And that was at dulook al-shams, when it leaned. So he stood and prayed the Zuhr, four rak'as. Ibn Mardawayh also related it by this route. And this is munqati' (broken in its chain).]]: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to me at the dulook of the sun, when the sun declined, and he led me in the Zuhr prayer." Its derivation is from al-dalk (rubbing), because a person rubs his eye when he looks at it. So if dulook means the decline (zawal), then the verse encompasses the five prayers; and if it means the setting (ghuroob), then the Zuhr and 'Asr have been excluded from it. Al-Ghasaq: the darkness, and it is the time of the 'Isha' prayer. "Wa Qur'an al-Fajr" (and the recitation of dawn): the Fajr prayer. It was named "Qur'an," which is recitation (al-qira'a), because recitation is a pillar (rukn) of it, just as it was named ruku' (bowing), sujud (prostration) and qunut (devotion). And this is a proof against Ibn 'Ulayya and al-Asamm in their claim that recitation is not a pillar. "Mashhudan" (witnessed): witnessed by the angels of the night and the day; these descend and those ascend, so it is at the end of the night's register and the beginning of the day's register. Or it is witnessed by a large number of worshippers customarily. Or it is due that it be witnessed by a large congregation. It is permissible that "Wa Qur'an al-Fajr" is an exhortation to lengthen the recitation in the Fajr prayer, because it is one in which people are crowded, so that people hear the Qur'an and the reward increases; and for this reason Fajr was the longest of the prayers in recitation. "Wa min al-layli" (and during part of the night): "And from the night, perform tahajjud with it as an extra (nafilah) for you." Tahajjud is abandoning sleep for prayer, and similar to it is ta'ththum (avoiding sin) and taharruj (avoiding wrongdoing). It is also said of sleep: tahajjada. "Nafilah laka": an additional act of worship for you beyond the five prayers. Nafilah was placed in the position of tahajjud, because tahajjud is an additional act of worship, so tahajjud and nafilah share one meaning. The meaning is that tahajjud is an addition for you upon the obligatory prayers, an obligation specific to you alone without others, since it is a voluntary act for them. "Maqaman mahmudan" is in the accusative as an adverbial of place (zarf), meaning: "It may be that your Lord raises you up on the Day of Resurrection and establishes you in a praiseworthy station." Or "yab'athaka" is taken to imply the meaning of "yuqimuka" (establishes you). It is also permissible that it be a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: that He raises you possessing a praiseworthy station. The meaning of "al-maqam al-mahmud": the station in which the one standing is praised, and everyone who sees it and recognizes it praises it; it is absolute in every matter deserving praise among kinds of honours. It was also said: the intended meaning is intercession (al-shafa'a), which is one type of what it encompasses. And from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: a station in which the first and last of creation praise you, and in which you are elevated above all creation: you ask and you are given, you intercede and your intercession is accepted; no one is except under your banner.

From Abu Hurayra, from the Prophet (ﷺ): it is the station in which I will intercede for my ummah [[Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shayba and al-Tirmidhi related it through Dawud ibn Yazid al-Awdi from his father from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His words, "It may be that your Lord raises you up to a praiseworthy station," and he was asked about it, and he said: "It is the intercession." And on this topic, from Anas in al-Bukhari's Tawhid; from Ibn 'Umar in his (al-Bukhari's) Zakat. And from Ibn Mas'ud in al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim, and it has another route in Ahmad and al-Hakim, expanded. And from Ka'b ibn Malik in al-Hakim. Its origin is in Muslim. And from Jabir in Ahmad and al-Hakim, and its connection and disconnection on al-Zuhri from 'Ali ibn al-Husayn is disputed. And from Abu Sa'id in al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Maja. And from 'Amr ibn Shu'ayb from his father from his grandfather in Ibn Mardawayh, expanded. And from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas in Ibn Mardawayh, through the narration of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan from Abu Hanifa from 'Abd al-Aziz ibn al-Rabi' from Mus'ab ibn Sa'd from his father, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) was asked about the praiseworthy station, and he said: It is the intercession."]]. And from Hudhayfa: Allah gathers the people in one plain, so that no soul speaks, and the first to be called is Muhammad (ﷺ), and he says: "Here I am at Your service, and I am happy to serve You; the evil is not attributed to You; the guided one is the one You have guided; Your servant is before You, by You and toward You; there is no refuge and no escape from You except toward You; You are blessed and exalted, glory be to You, Lord of the House." He said: this is His saying, "It may be that your Lord raises you up to a praiseworthy station" [[al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, Ibn Abi Shayba, al-Tabari, Abu Ya'la, al-Bazzar and Abu Nu'aym in his biography of Hudhayfa in al-Hilya, all through the route of Shu'ba and Isra'il, both from Abu Ishaq, who said: I heard 'Utba ibn Zafar say: I heard Hudhayfa say, "Allah gathers the people," and he mentioned it.]].

The passage has been read as *mudkhal* and *mukhraj*, with a damma or a fatha on the first letter. Both are the verbal noun (*masdar*), and the sense of the fatha is: "Cause me to enter, so I enter an entry of truthfulness." That is, cause me to enter the grave with an entry that is pleasing, in purity and goodness, free of evil deeds, and cause me to come out of it at the Resurrection with an exit that is pleasing, met with honour, secure from wrath. This is indicated by its being mentioned directly after the mention of the Resurrection.

It was also said: it was revealed when he was commanded to migrate, and the meaning is his entering Madina and his leaving Makka. It was also said: his entering Makka openly, as a conqueror over it, by conquest, and his leaving it secure from the polytheists. It was also said: his entering the cave and his leaving it safe. It was also said: his entering into the great matter with which he was entrusted, which is prophethood, and his leaving it having discharged what he was charged with, without neglect. It was also said: it refers to obedience. It was also said: it is general to everything he enters and is involved in, whether a matter or a place.

"Authority" (*sultan*) here means a proof that supports me against those who oppose me, or a kingdom and a strong might that aids Islam against disbelief and makes it prevail over it. His supplication was answered by His words ﴿And God will protect you from the people﴾ [5:67], ﴿for the party of God, they are the victorious﴾ [5:56], ﴿that He may make it prevail over all religion﴾ [9:33], and ﴿He will surely make them successors in the earth﴾ [24:55]. And His promise was that He would surely strip the kingdom of Persia and Rome and give it to him.

It is related from him (ﷺ) that he appointed ʿAttab ibn Asid over the people of Makka and said: "Go, for I have appointed you over the people of God." He was severe toward the doubtful and gentle toward the believer. He said: "By God, I do not know of anyone who stays away from the congregational prayer except that I will strike off his neck, for only a hypocrite stays away from prayer." The people of Makka said: "O Messenger of God, you have appointed over the people of God ʿAttab ibn Asid, a coarse bedouin!" He (ﷺ) said: "I saw in a dream, as one who sleeps sees, that ʿAttab ibn Asid came to the gate of Paradise, took hold of the ring of the door, and shook it violently until it was opened for him, and he entered it. Thus God strengthened Islam through him, by his support of the Muslims against those who wished to wrong them. That is the ﴿victorious authority﴾ [17:80]."

[Al-Tha'labi related it with his chain from al-Kalbi, who said: ʿAttab ibn Asid, whom the Messenger of God (ﷺ) appointed over the people of Makka, and he mentioned it in the same way. Ibn Mardawayh related it by way of Isma'il ibn Khalifa al-Kalbi, from Abu Salih, from Ibn ʿAbbas, without the hadith at its end.]

Around the House (the Ka'bah) there were three hundred and sixty idols, each tribe having its own idol opposite it. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the tribes of the Arabs used to make pilgrimage to them and sacrifice to them. So the House complained to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and said:

"O my Lord, how long will these idols be worshipped around me, besides You?" Then Allah revealed to the House: "I shall bring about for you a new cycle, and I shall fill you with prostrating faces who will come to you ﴿at a gentle pace﴾ [[On the phrase "يدفون إليك دفيف النسور" (they will hasten to you with the swift gliding of vultures): in the Sihah, "al-Dafif" is the dabib, which is a gentle walking pace, and in it "al-'Ajj" is raising the voice, and one says "'ajja ya'iju 'ajijan." (Ea)]], longing for you as a bird longs for its eggs. There will be a clamour around you of the talbiyah (the pilgrim's call, "Here I am, O Allah")."

When this verse was revealed on the day of the Conquest, Jibril, peace be upon him, said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Take your staff and throw it." So he went to each idol, one by one, poking at its eye with the staff and saying: "The Truth has come and falsehood has vanished" ﴿Truly falsehood is ever bound to vanish﴾. Each idol would fall on its face until he had thrown them all down. Only the idol of Khuza'ah remained, atop the Ka'bah, and it was made of yellow glass. He said: "O 'Ali, throw it down." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lifted him up until he climbed and threw it down, and it broke. The people of Makkah then marvelled and said:

"We have never seen a man more skilled in magic than Muhammad" (ﷺ).

[[I did not find this. Al-Nasa'i and al-Hakim related through the route of Ibn Abi Maryam from 'Ali, who said: "I set out with the Prophet ﷺ until we came to the Ka'bah, and he said to me, 'Sit,' so I sat. Then he climbed onto my shoulders and I rose with him..." and the hadith continues. There is nothing in it that this was at the Conquest of Makkah, nor a recitation of the verse. Al-Nasa'i [thus in both originals, Ed.]]]

The complaint of the House and the revelation to it are a figurative representation and imaginative portrayal.

﴿And falsehood vanished﴾ means it went away and perished, from the expression "zahaqat nafsuhu" (his soul departed) when it came out. "The Truth" means Islam.

"Falsehood" means shirk (polytheism). ﴿Was ever bound to vanish﴾ means it was ever dissolving, not lasting, at all times.

And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers (Qur'an is read with both light and emphatic pronunciation of the verb). "Min" here is explanatory (lil-tabyin), as in His saying: "from the idols" (min al-awthan).

Or it is partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: whatever part of the Qur'an has been sent down is a healing for the believers, through which they increase in faith and set right their religion. Its position with respect to them is thus the position of cure with respect to the sick. And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever does not seek healing through the Qur'an, may Allah not grant him healing." [Al-Tha'labi related it through the route of Ahmad ibn al-Harith al-Ghassani: Sakina bint al-Ja'd narrated to us, she said: I heard Raja' al-Ghanawi say: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, and he mentioned it.]

"And it increases the wrongdoers in nothing but loss" means a decrease for them, because of their denial of it and their disbelief, as in His saying: "But it increased them in filth upon their filth."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 83–84:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself (نَأى بِجانِبِهِ)...﴾ Translation of the text: When We bestow favour upon man with health and abundance, he turns away from the remembrance of God, as if he were independent of Him and self-sufficient. ﴿And distances himself﴾ is an emphasis on the turning away, because turning away from something means showing it the back of one's face. Distancing with the side (al-nana bi-l-janib) means that one turns one's side away from it and presents one's back to it, and the intended meaning is arrogance, because that is the habit of the arrogant. ﴿And when evil touches him, whether poverty, sickness, or any of the calamities, he is desperate (yaʼus), utterly hopeless of the mercy of God.﴾ ﴿Indeed, none despairs of the mercy of God except the disbelieving people.﴾

It is read also: wa-na'a bi-janibihi (وناء بجانبه), with the lam placed before the ayn, like the saying "ra'a" for "ra'y"... and it is permissible that it derive from "nā'a," meaning "nahada" (to rise). 

﴿Say: Each acts according to his own manner (shākilah)﴾, that is, according to his own school of thought and his method, which conforms to his state in guidance and error, from the expression "a road with shawākil," which are the paths branching off from it. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way (sabīl)﴾, that is, whose school of thought and method is most upright.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 83–84:

﴿And when We bestow favour upon man, he turns away and distances himself (نَأى بِجانِبِهِ)...﴾ Translation of the text: When We bestow favour upon man with health and abundance, he turns away from the remembrance of God, as if he were independent of Him and self-sufficient. ﴿And distances himself﴾ is an emphasis on the turning away, because turning away from something means showing it the back of one's face. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿Your Lord knows best who is best guided in the way (sabīl)﴾, that is, whose school of thought and method is most upright.

The majority view is that it is the spirit that is in living beings. They asked him about its reality, and he informed them that it is of the command of God (ﷺ?) — no, rendered as: "it is of the affair of God, that is, of what He has kept to the knowledge of Himself alone." And from Ibn Abi Buraydah: "The Prophet (ﷺ) passed away without knowing the spirit."[[Al-Wahidi mentions this in al-Wasit from Abdullah ibn Buraydah with this wording, in a hadith whose isnad was not mentioned before.]]

It is also said that it is a great spiritual creation, greater than an angel. It is said that it is Jibril (peace be upon him). It is said that it is the Qur'an.

﴿Say: The spirit is of the command of my Lord﴾, that is, of His revelation and His speech, not of human speech. The Jews sent to the Quraysh, saying: "Ask him about the People of the Cave, about Dhu al-Qarnayn, and about the spirit. If he answers them or remains silent, then he is not a prophet; but if he answers some and remains silent about others, then he is a prophet." So he explained the two stories to them and left the matter of the spirit undetermined, and it is undetermined in the Torah. So they regretted their question.[[I have not found it in this form. Ibn Hisham mentions it in the Sirah from Ziyad from Abu Ishaq, and al-Bayhaqi likewise related it in al-Dala'il through that chain: "The people of Makkah sent a group of them to the Jews, asking them about things by which they would test the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said: Ask him about three things; if he knows them, he is a prophet. Ask him about peoples who went into the earth and it is not known what became of them ... the story in full."]]

﴿And you have been given only a little of knowledge﴾: is the address to them, or is he (the Prophet) included in it? He said:

"Rather, we and you have not been given of knowledge except a little." They said: "How strange is your matter! At one time you say ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good﴾, and at another you say this."[[Al-Tha'labi mentions it in his tafsir of Luqman without any chain or narrator. Ibn Mardawayh related it through Ali ibn Asim from Dawud ibn Abi Hind from Ikrimah, who I do not know except from Ibn Abbas, who said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿And you have been given only a little of knowledge﴾, the Jews said: We have been given much knowledge. We have been given the Torah, and whoever is given the Torah has been given much good. So God the Exalted revealed ﴿Say: If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord, the sea would be exhausted﴾."]] Then it was revealed: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens﴾.

What they said is not necessarily valid, because smallness and greatness are relative to what they are attributed to. Something is described as small when compared to what is above it, and as great when compared to what is below it. So the wisdom that a servant is given is much good in itself, but when it is compared to the knowledge of God, it is little.

It is also said that it is an address to the Jews specifically, because they said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "We have been given the Torah, and in it is wisdom, and we have recited ﴿And whoever is given wisdom has been given much good﴾." So it was said to them: The knowledge of the Torah is little in comparison to the knowledge of God.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 86–87:

[The passage as given begins mid-argument in the original commentary; the translation follows the text exactly.]

لَنَذْهَبَنَّ: the answer of an implied oath (qasam mahdhuf), which stands in place of the answer of the conditional (jaza' al-shart). The lam that enters upon inna is the lam of preparation for the oath (lam al-muwatta'a lil-qasam).

The meaning: if We will, We shall indeed take away the Qur'an, erasing it from the breasts and the codices, so that We leave no trace of it, and you remain as you were, not knowing what the Book is.

ثُمَّ لا تَجِدُ لَكَ بعد الذهاب بِهِ من يتوكل علينا باسترداده وإعادته محفوظا مستورا

"Then you will not find for yourself, after its taking away, anyone who will take it upon himself (to act) on Our behalf in retrieving it and restoring it preserved and protected."

إِلَّا رَحْمَةً مِنْ رَبِّكَ

"Except a mercy from your Lord": that is, except that your Lord has mercy on you and returns it to you. As if His mercy is what takes it upon itself to return it. Or it may be an exceptive clause of the disjunct type (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but a mercy from your Lord has left it untaken away.

This is a favour from God Almighty, by the continued preservation of the Qur'an after the great favour of its being sent down and of its being committed to memory. So every person of knowledge should not be heedless of these two favours and of giving thanks for them: the first is God's favour to him in preserving knowledge and its firm establishment in his breast, and the second is His favour to him in the continuance of what is memorized.

And from Ibn Mas'ud:

"The first thing you will lose of your religion is trustworthiness, and the last thing you will lose is the prayer. People will pray while having no religion. Indeed this Qur'an, one morning you will find that there is nothing of it left among you." A man said: "How could that be, when we have fixed it in our hearts and fixed it in our codices, teaching it to our sons and our sons teaching it to their sons?" He said: "It will be taken away in the night, and people will wake up in the morning empty of it; the codices will be lifted and what is in the hearts will be removed."

[Narrated by Abd al-Razzaq and, by his route, al-Tabarani; also narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Mardawayh, all by the route of Shaddad ibn Ma'qil from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, and he added at its end: then Abdullah recited, "And if We willed, We would surely take away that which We have revealed to you."]

﴿لَا يَأْتُونَ﴾ is the answer to a suppressed oath. Were it not for the preparatory *lam* (*al-lam al-muwatta'a*, the lam that introduces an oath), it could have been the answer to the conditional clause, as in the line of poetry: "He says: 'Neither is my absent [wealth] lost, nor my sacred [honor]'" (the verse's first half, *yaqūlu lā gha'ib māli wa lā ḥaram*). The explanation of this witness has been given in the first volume, p. 537, so refer to it if you wish. Its editor, may God have mercy on him, said so.

This is because the conditional clause is in the past tense. The meaning is: even if they joined forces to bring about something like this Qur'an in its eloquence, its excellent arrangement and its composition, and among them were the original Arabs (*al-'Arab al-'āriba*), masters of eloquent expression, they would still be unable to produce its like.

How strange it is that the newcomers (*al-nawābit*, the young and inexperienced; in *al-Ṣiḥāḥ* of al-Jawharī: "*al-nawābit min al-aḥdāth*," those new to affairs; and in it: "a *ghamr* man is one who has not been tested") and their claim that the Qur'an is eternal, while they acknowledge that it is inimitable, [[Mahmud said: "How strange are the newcomers and their claim that the Qur'an is eternal, while they acknowledge that it is inimitable…" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said:

One sign of the author's departure from the way of the fair-minded is that he deceives the weak-minded on this question, which has spread across the earth in its prominence and currency. Yet he is content to feign ignorance of the position of the people (the Sunnis), which is that the meaning of the expressions is an eternal attribute subsisting in the Essence of the Exalted Creator, which is called "Qur'an." It is also applied to its indicators, namely these eloquent words and noble verses, which are called "Qur'an." According to them, what is inimitable is the indicator and not the meaning indicated. Yet they avoid saying that it is created, for two reasons. The first is that it is an expression that causes misunderstanding. The second is that the pious predecessors (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*) refrained from it, so they followed their traces and borrowed their lights.

How many a belief there is that one does not state, for fear of creating in others an impression of something not permissible to believe. There is no link between belief and expression, and no esteem for one who holds that belief or for one who insists on holding others to it. ﴿And God speaks the truth, and He guides to the way﴾ (33:4).]] (it is a matter of) the fact that inimitability arises only where there is power (*qudra*), so one says: God is capable of creating bodies, and servants are incapable of it. As for the impossible, where there is no room for power and no part for it in it, like "the second of the eternal," one does not say of the agent that he is incapable of it, nor that it is inimitable. Had one said so, it would be permissible to describe God as incapable, since He is not described as having power over the impossible, unless they were to be stubborn and say that He is capable of the impossible. [[The phrase "the chief of their possessions is stubbornness" is not as he said, may God forgive him. Rather, the chief of what they hold is clinging to the Book and the Sunna, and seeking out realities.]] For the chief of what they possess is stubbornness and the inversion of realities.

And indeed, We have turned about (ṣarrafnā), repeated and reiterated (raddadnā wa-karrarnā), within this Qur'an, from every example (mathal), that is, from every meaning which is like an example in its strangeness and its beauty.

Al-kufūr (ingratitude/disbelief): al-juḥūd (denial, obstinate rejection). If it is said: how is it permissible to say fa-abā akthar al-nās illā kufūran (yet most of the people refused except to deny), while it is not permissible to say ḍarabtu illā Zaydan (I struck no one except Zayd)? I say: because abā (refused) is interpreted (mutaʾawwal) as negation, as if it were said: fa-lam yarḍū illā kufūran (so they were not content except with denial).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 90–93:

When the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an became clear, and the other miracles and clear proofs were added to it, and the argument bound them and they were overcome, they began to make excuses by demanding signs. This is the behavior of one who is stunned, refuted, and stumbling in the skirts of bewilderment. They said: ﴿We will not believe you until...﴾ ﴿...you cause a spring to gush (tafjur) forth for us from the earth﴾, meaning the land of Makkah, ﴿a flowing spring﴾, a abundant spring whose nature is to gush with water without cutting off. It is the form "yaf'ul" from "nabaʿa al-ma'" (the water sprang forth), like "ya'bub" from "ʿabba al-ma'" (the water flowed abundantly). Tafjur is also read with the lighter form (tujjir ... tafjur). ﴿As you claimed﴾, meaning the saying of God, Exalted is He: ﴿If We will, We shall cause the earth to swallow them, or We shall drop upon them fragments (kisafan) from the heaven﴾. It is read as "kisfan" with a sukun on the sin, the plural of "kisfah," like "sidrah" and "sidr." With a fatha on it, it means ﴿a witness (qabilan)﴾, meaning a guarantor for what you say, a witness to its truth. The meaning is: ﴿or you bring God and the angels as a guarantor (qabilan)﴾, like the saying of the poet:

"...I and my father were cleared of it..."

It is by al-Farazdaq. He says: he hurled at me a matter from which I and my father are innocent. The verb "kana" is here stripped of the sense of past time, and the predicate of the father is omitted because it is indicated by what precedes it, and the conjunction is the conjunction of sentences. "Bari'an" (innocent) is in the sense of being placed first, so it does not follow that anything of the conjoined precedes the thing conjoined to. This is the view of the majority. Some have permitted that "wa-waldi" is conjoined to the subject of "kana," so that "bari'an" is its predicate, with the predicate of its subject omitted, or the reverse, and the conjunction is one of single words. It is also permissible that "bari'an" is a predicate about both of them, because "fa'il" (in the form "fa'il") is used for the singular and the plural, being in the pattern of the verbal noun, like "suhayl," "dujaj," "nahib," and "nasib," though its use in the sense of "fa'il" is rare. "Jawl al-tawa" (with a dammah) is the side of the walled well. The meaning is that he hurled at me a matter that returns upon himself, as if he hurled at me a stone while he was at the bottom of the well, so it returns upon him. This is a metaphor for requiting him with a matter greater than what he hurled at me. It is also permissible that the matter with which he hurled at him is characterized by the thrower, and this is more suitable to the comparison.

It is also narrated as "wa-min ajl al-tawa" (because of the well). So let it be verified.

﴿...for I and Qayyar in it are strangers﴾ [Editor's note: the explanation of this witness was given in volume one, page 629; refer to it if you wish.]

Or [the angels come] as a counterpart (muqabilan), like "al-ʿashir" in the sense of "al-muʿashir" (the companion), and similar. ﴿Why were the angels not sent down upon us, or why do we not see our Lord?﴾ Or a group, as a circumstantial clause from the angels. ﴿From ornament (zukhruf)﴾, meaning from gold, ﴿in the sky﴾, meaning in the ascending paths of the heaven, so the modifier is omitted.

It is said: "raqiya" in the ladder and in the rank. ﴿And we will not believe in your ascent (ruqiyyika)﴾, meaning we will not believe because of your ascent, ﴿until you send down upon us a book from heaven that confirms you﴾. It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Umayyah said:

"We will not believe you until you take a ladder to the sky and climb it while we watch, until you reach it, then come to us with a published document, with four angels accompanying you who testify for you that you are as you say."

They did not intend by these demands anything but obstinacy and contentiousness. Even if every sign had come to them, they would have said: ﴿This is magic﴾, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Even if We sent down upon you a book on paper, and they touched it with their hands, those who disbelieve would say, "This is nothing but clear magic"﴾, and ﴿Even if We opened for them a gate from heaven, and they continued to ascend through it, they would say, "Our eyes have only been dazzled; rather we are a people bewitched"﴾. When they denied the lasting sign, which is the Qur'an and the rest of the signs, and these are no less than what they demanded, rather they are greater, there was no way to their insight. ﴿Say: Glory be to my Lord﴾. It is read: "Qala subhana rabbi" (he said), meaning the Messenger said it. ﴿Glory be to my Lord﴾ is an expression of wonder at their demands upon him. ﴿Am I anything but a messenger, a human like them?﴾ The messengers did not come to their peoples except with what God manifests to them of signs. So the matter of signs is not in my hands; it is up to God. Why, then, do you choose them over me?

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 94–95:

Anna (أَنْ) the first is in the accusative as the second object of mana'a (منع, "to prevent"). The second is in the nominative as its subject (fa'il). Al-huda (الْهُدى) means the revelation (al-wahy), i.e.:

Nothing prevented them from believing in the Qur'an and in the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) except a doubt that wavered in their breasts, namely their denial that God would send a human being as a messenger. The hamza in ʾa-baʿatha Allahu (أَبَعَثَ اللَّهُ, "has God sent...?") is for denunciation (lil-inkar), and what they denied, its opposite is what is reprehensible in the sight of God, because it is a requirement of His wisdom that He sends the angel of revelation only to beings like them, or to the prophets. Then He affirmed this by saying: ﴿If there were angels in the earth walking calmly, [as they walk], then We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾. [Mahmud said: "its meaning is, if they were walking as humans walk and not flying with their wings to the heaven... etc." Ahmad said: His statement here contains a good answer to a presumed objection, which is the words of someone who says: the mere existence of angels on earth suits sending an angel to them, so what is the benefit of this addition? So its answer is what has preceded, and God is the Granter of success.]

They would hear from its inhabitants and learn what must be known, being at rest (mutma'innin), settled (qarrin) in the earth. ﴿We would have sent down to them from the heaven an angel as a messenger﴾, who would teach them good and guide them to the right paths. As for humans, they are not in this position; rather an angel is sent to one chosen among them for prophethood, and that chosen one undertakes calling them and guiding them. If you ask: Is it permissible for them to be human and angel, in the accusative as circumstantial states (hal) of "messenger"? I say: it is a good aspect, but the meaning is more apt to the other.

Witness between me and you (that I have conveyed what I was sent with to you, and that you denied and obstinately opposed). Indeed He is ever Aware of His servants, Seeing (Khabir), knowing their conditions, so He will recompense them. This is a consolation for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a warning to the disbelievers. "Shahidan" is either a specification (tamyiz) or a circumstantial accusative (hal).

Note: the text as given contains a phrase, "والمنذرين", that appears to be a scribal or transmission variant in this line; I have rendered it as it stands in the Arabic.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verses 97–98:

﴿And whomever Allah guides, he is the one guided; and whomever He leaves astray, you will not find for them protectors other than Him.﴾ Whoever Allah guides, that is, whom He grants success and shows kindness (luṭf), he is the one truly guided, because He only shows kindness to those whom He knows kindness will benefit. And whoever He leaves astray, that is, whom He forsakes, ﴿you will not find for them protectors (awliyāʾ), helpers.﴾ ﴿On their faces﴾ is like His saying: ﴿On the Day they are dragged into the Fire on their faces﴾ (Qur'an 54:48). It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "How will they walk on their faces?" He said: "Indeed, the One who made them walk on their feet is able to make them walk on their faces."

﴿Blind, dumb and deaf﴾, as they were in the world: they do not perceive (the truth), nor do they speak the truth, and they feign deafness to hearing it. So in the Hereafter they are likewise: they do not see what would gladden their eyes, nor do they hear what would delight their ears [[His saying "nor do they hear what would delight their ears": in the Ṣiḥāḥ: "lidhdhtu al-shayʾ" (with kasra): I found it delightful.]] nor do they speak what would be accepted from them. ﴿And whoever was blind in this (world), he will be blind in the Hereafter.﴾ It is also permissible that they be gathered with their senses impaired from the place of standing to the Fire after the reckoning. For He has informed us in another place that they will speak and talk. ﴿Whenever it dies down, We increase for them the blaze﴾: whenever the Fire's flame subsides after consuming their skins and flesh and destroying them, they are given new skins, and it blazes again, fierce. It is as if, since they denied resurrection after annihilation, God made their recompense that the Fire be set upon their parts, consuming and annihilating them, and then He restores them. They remain in continual annihilation and restoration, so that this increases their remorse over denying the resurrection. It is also more fitting for retribution against the denier. This is indicated by His saying: ﴿That is their recompense﴾ up to His saying: ﴿"Shall we indeed be resurrected in a new creation?"﴾ (Qur'an 17:98–99).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 99:

If you ask: "On what is the phrase ﴿and He has appointed for them a term﴾ conjoined?" I answer: it is conjoined to His saying ﴿Do they not see that Allah, who created the heavens and the earth, is able to create the like of them?﴾, because the meaning is that they have known, by the proof of reason, that whoever is able to create the heavens and the earth is able to create the likes of them from among mankind, since they are not stronger in creation than those [heavens and earth], as He says: ﴿Are you stronger in creation or is the heaven?﴾ [79:27]. ﴿And He has appointed for them a term, about which there is no doubt﴾, and it is death or the Resurrection. Yet they refused, despite the clarity of the proof, except to deny.

Had the particle law (لَوْ) by its nature been meant to enter upon verbs rather than nouns, then a verb must follow it in "law antum tamlikūn" (﴿لَوْ أَنتُمْ تَمْلِكُونَ﴾), and its estimated form is "law tamlikūn." So the verb "tamlikūn" is suppressed by way of a condition of explanation (ʿalā sharīṭat al-tafsīr), and the detached pronoun "antum," which replaces the attached pronoun that is the wāw, is put in its place, because the verbal element attached to it has dropped out. Thus "antum" is the subject (fāʿil) of the suppressed verb, and "tamlikūn" is its explanation. This is the aspect required by the science of grammatical inflection (ʿilm al-iʿrāb). As for what the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-bayān) requires, it is that "antum tamlikūn" indicates restriction (ikhtiṣāṣ), and that people are the ones specifically characterized by extreme niggardliness. A similar usage is the verse of Ḥātim:

"Law dhāt sawār laṭamatnī"

and the verse of al-Mutalammis:

"Wa law ghayr akhwālī arādū naqīṣatī [[Wa law ghayr ikhwānī arādū naqīṣatī ... juʿaftu lahum fawqa al-ʿarānīn mīsamā

Wa hal kuntu illā mithla qāṭiʿin kaffahu ... bikaffin lahu ukhrā ʿalayhi taqaddamā]]"

Al-Mutalammis was the maternal uncle of Ṭarafa ibn al-ʿAbd. "Law" is one of the particles of conditioning (ḥurūf al-sharṭ), so whenever a verb is within its scope, it has the greater claim to it. Thus "ghayr ikhwānī" is the subject of a suppressed verb which the mentioned one explains, meaning: "and if the others than my brothers wished..." It is also narrated as "akhwālī" (my maternal uncles). "Naqīṣatī" means my wrong-doing: "if I branded them with humiliation, branding them visibly, as if upon the noses," and he specified these because they cannot be hidden. "Al-mīsam" is the instrument of branding with fire, and what is meant is its mark, which is the sign (simma).

"Wa hal" is an interrogative of denial, meaning: "if I were to requite my brothers, I would be none other than one who cut off his own hand with his other hand." The word "kaff" (hand) may be masculine or feminine, so for this reason he described it as having advanced over the other hand, transgressed against it, and described it as "ukhrā" (other). The contrast between the two hands supports the narration "ikhwānī" with the nūn.

This is because the first verb, when it was dropped for the sake of the explanatory element, and the speech appeared in the form of a subject and predicate. "Raḥmat Allāh" means His provision and all His other blessings upon His creatures. This attribute of niggardliness has reached an extreme that imagination cannot attain.

It is said: it is addressed to the people of Makkah, who proposed what they proposed concerning the spring and the rivers and other things, and that if they possessed the treasuries of provisions they would be niggardly with them, "qatūran," meaning constricted, stingy, miserly. If you say: Can "la-amsaktum" be estimated to have an object (maf'ūl)?

I say: No, because its meaning is "la-bakhiltum" (you would have been stingy), from your saying to the miser: "mumsik."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 101:

Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him and his father) said: They are the staff, the hand, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the stone, the sea, and the mount (al-Tur) which He raised over the Children of Israel. And al-Hasan said: the flood, the years of famine, and the shortage of fruits, in place of the stone, the sea, and the mount. It is related from ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAziz that he asked Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, and he mentioned the tongue and the effacing [[His saying "he mentioned the tongue and the effacing" probably refers to the knot that was in his tongue, which he loosened, as al-Khazin counted it. As for the effacing (tams), it is the answering of his supplication in His saying, "Our Lord, efface their wealth" (Qur'an 10:88), and the mention of what is in the reply alludes to that. (ʿ)]]. ʿUmar said to him: "How could a jurist be other than this? Boy, bring out that bag." He brought it out and shook it, and there were eggs broken in two halves, a walnut broken, garlic [[His saying "garlic" (fawm): in the Sihah, "al-fawm" is garlic; it is also called wheat (hintah). (ʿ)]], chickpeas and lentils, all of them stones.

It is related from Safwan ibn ʿAssal that some Jews asked the Prophet ﷺ about that, and he said: Allah revealed to Musa: "Say to the Children of Israel: Do not associate anything with Allah, do not steal, do not commit adultery, do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except by right, do not practice magic, do not consume usury, do not walk with an innocent person to a ruler so that he may kill him, do not slander a chaste woman, do not flee from the battle line; and you, O Jews in particular, do not transgress on the Sabbath." [[Related by al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and al-Hakim; and Ahmad, Ishaq, Abu Yaʿla and al-Tabarani, all of them through the narration of ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam from Safwan ibn ʿAssal that two Jews, one of them said to his companion, "Come, let us go to this Prophet and ask him." The other said, "Do not call him a prophet, for if he hears you, he will have four eyes." So they came to the Prophet ﷺ and asked him, and he mentioned the hadith. None of them said "Allah revealed to Musa: say to the Children of Israel," and the rest is the same. ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam grew old and his memory deteriorated, and what was asked about was the ten words, because their number is ten, not the nine signs, because the ten are commandments like these, and the nine are proofs against Pharaoh and his people. (ʿ)]]

"So ask the Children of Israel" (Qur'an 17:101). We said to him: Ask the Children of Israel, that is, ask them from Pharaoh, and say to him: Send the Children of Israel with me. Or: ask them about their faith and the state of their religion. Or: ask them to support you, so that their hearts and hands are with you. And the reading of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ supports this: "fasala Bani Isra'il," in the past tense without hamza, and this is the dialect of Quraysh. It has also been said:

O Messenger of Allah, ask the believers among the Children of Israel, namely ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, about the signs, so that they may increase in certainty and tranquillity of heart, for when the proofs converge, that is stronger and firmer, like the saying of Ibrahim: "but that my heart may be at rest" (Qur'an 2:260). If you say: With what is "idh jaahum" connected? I say: As for the first aspect, it is connected to the omitted saying, meaning "We said to him: ask them when he came to them," or to "ask" in the second reading. As for the last, it is connected to "We gave" (ataynā), or to an implied "remember," or to "they will inform you." The meaning of "idh jaahum" is: when he came to their fathers. "Maswur" (bewitched): your mind has been bewitched and confused.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 17, verse 102–104:

﴿Indeed you know, O Pharaoh, that none sent these signs except the Lord of the heavens and the earth, as clear evidences.﴾ But you are obstinate and arrogant. A similar expression is: ﴿And they denied them wrongfully and arrogantly, though their souls were convinced of them.﴾ It is also read "ʿalimta" (you know) with a ḍammah on the ʿayn-less form, "ʿulimta," meaning: "I am not bewitched as you have described me; rather, I am certain of the truth of the matter."

And ﴿that the Lord of the heavens and the earth sent these signs﴾. Then he (Musa) struck his assumption against your assumption, as if he said: "If you think I am bewitched, then I think you are ruined and destroyed (mathbur, hālik), and my assumption is more correct than yours, because mine has a clear sign, namely your denial of what you knew to be true and your arrogance toward the signs of God after their clarity. As for your assumption, it is pure falsehood, because your saying, while you know the truth of my matter, ﴿Indeed I think you are bewitched﴾, is the speech of a liar." Al-Farrāʾ said: mathbūr means "turned away from good and sealed upon your heart," from the expression "mā thabaraka ʿan hādhā?" meaning "What prevented and turned you away from this?"

Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read: ﴿Indeed, I think you, O Pharaoh, are surely ruined,﴾ with "inna" as the lightened (mukhaffafah) form and the "lām" as the lām al-fāriqah (the distinguishing lām).

﴿So he intended to drive them out of the land,﴾ that is, Pharaoh intended to expel Musa and his people from the land of Egypt and drive them out of it, or to banish them from the face of the earth by killing and extermination. ﴿But We drowned him and those with him all together. And We said to the Children of Israel after him: "Dwell in the land,"﴾ the land from which Pharaoh intended to expel you. ﴿So when the promise of the Hereafter comes, We will bring you forth as a mixed multitude,﴾ meaning the establishment of the Hour, ﴿gathering you together, you and them, then He will judge between you and distinguish between your fortunate and your wretched.﴾ And al-lafīf (the mixed multitude) means: groups from various tribes.
