And with truth We sent it down, and with truth it descended. We did not send down the Qur'an except with the wisdom that necessitated its sending down, and it did not descend except joined with truth and wisdom, since it includes guidance to every good. Or: We did not send it down from heaven except with truth, guarded by the watch of the angels, and it did not descend upon the Messenger except guarded by them from the confusion of the devils. ﴿And We did not send you except as a bringer of good news and a warner.﴾ Your duty is nothing beyond that, [such as] compulsion in religion or the like.

And (We sent down) the Qur'an, which is in the accusative case, governed by a verb implied by the verb that explains it: "We divided it" (faraqnahu). Ubayy read it as "farraqnahu" with the doubled letter, meaning: We made its descent divided and spread out over time (munajjaman).

It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, that he read it with the doubled letter and said: "It was not sent down in two or three days; rather, between its beginning and its end there were twenty years," meaning that "faraqa" with the single letter indicates a close (or nearer) separation.

"'Ala mukth" (at a steady pace), with the vowel either fatha or damma: slowly, unhurriedly, and deliberately.

"And We sent it down in stages" (tanzilan), in accordance with the events as they occurred.

Say: "Believe in it or do not believe." This is a command to turn away from them, to disregard them and to hold their affairs in contempt, and to pay no heed to them, to their faith, or to their refusal to accept it. Even if they do not enter into faith or accept the Qur'an, they are people of ignorance and polytheism. Yet those better and more excellent than them, namely the scholars who have read the scriptures and know what revelation (wahy) and the sacred laws (shara'i') are, have already believed in it and affirmed it. For them it has been established that he is the Arab Prophet promised in their scriptures. So when it is recited to them, they fall down prostrate, glorifying God in reverence for His command and for the fulfilment of what He promised in the revealed books, and of the good news of the sending of Muhammad ﷺ and the descent of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise in His words: ﴿Indeed the promise of our Lord is surely fulfilled.﴾ ...... ﴿And it increases them in humility﴾, that is, the Qur'an increases them in softness of heart and moistness of eye.

If you ask: what is the reason given by ﴿Indeed those who were given knowledge before it﴾? I answer: it may be a justification for His words "Believe in it or do not believe," and it may be a justification for "Say," by way of consolation for the Messenger of God ﷺ and to comfort his heart, as if it were said: "Console yourself regarding the faith of the ignorant with the faith of the scholars." On the first reading, the meaning is: "If you do not believe in it, then one better than you has believed in it."

If you ask: what is the meaning of falling down upon the chin (al-kharur lil-dhaqan)? I answer: it means falling onto the face. The chin (dhaqan), which is the meeting point of the two jaws, is mentioned because the one who prostrates first meets the earth with his chin. 

If you ask: the preposition of elevation (harf al-isti'la') is clear in meaning when you say "kharra 'ala wajhihi" (he fell upon his face) and "'ala dhaqanihi" (upon his chin), so what is the meaning of the lam in "kharra lidhaqanihi" and "li-wajhihi" (fell for/onto his chin and his face)? He said:

*So he fell prone, for both his hands and his mouth*

*At the Day of al-Kilab our spears had removed (him) ...
Sharahbil, when he swore an oath, a swearing one:*

*"He will surely snatch our spears," so he removed him,
Abu Hanash, from the back of a long, hard-hoofed mare.*

*He reached him with the spear, then turned back to him,
So he fell prone, for both his hands and his mouth.*

(This is attributed to Jabir al-Tha'labi. It is also said that the third line belongs to Shurayh al-'Absi, and it is also said to Zuhayr. Al-Kilab, with a dammah, is the name of the place of the battle. Ali means he swore. Al-shanqa' means a long mare, and al-saldam, with a kasra on the unpointed letters, means strong. It is also narrated as "thumma ith'na lahu," and the original is "inthana," where the nun was assimilated after being changed to a thaa'. If it were recited as "thumma a'tani" (from ataani, "came to me") and "tamahhala" (he delayed), it would be permissible. It is narrated as "dalafat lahu bil-rumh min tahti bazzihi" (I advanced to him with the spear from beneath his armour), and as "shaqqafat lahu bil-rumh jaybu qamisihi" (I pierced for him with the spear the collar of his shirt). The variation in the narrations is likely due to the variation in the speakers. Al-tanawul means taking hold, so the meaning is: he reached him and stabbed him with the spear, as if he had seized him; then "inthana lahu" means he stabbed him again, so he fell prostrate. He made it so for his hands and his mouth, because they are what first meet the earth when he falls upon his face. The lam here has the meaning of 'ala, as the grammarians have stated, though al-Nahhas denied it. Dalafa dalfan, like ta'iba ta'aban, means he advanced quickly and shortened his steps. Jaybu qamisihi is a metaphor for his chest, because if the collar of the shirt is torn by the spear, the chest has been torn.)

I say: its meaning is that He made their chins and faces for the falling and singled them out for it, because the lam denotes exclusivity (ikhtisas).

If you ask: why did He repeat "yakhurrun lil-adhqan" (they fall upon their chins)? I answer: because the two states differ. They fall while prostrating, and they fall while weeping.

So he fell prone, for both his hands and his mouth.*

Al-Kilab, with a dammah, is the name of the place of the battle. Ali means he swore. Al-shanqa' means a long mare, and al-saldam, with a kasra on the unpointed letters, means strong. It is also narrated as "thumma ith'na lahu," and the original is "inthana," where the nun was assimilated after being changed to a thaa'. If it were recited as "thumma a'tani" (from ataani, "came to me") and "tamahhala" (he delayed), it would be permissible. It is narrated as "dalafat lahu bil-rumh min tahti bazzihi" (I advanced to him with the spear from beneath his armour), and as "shaqqafat lahu bil-rumh jaybu qamisihi" (I pierced for him with the spear the collar of his shirt). The variation in the narrations is likely due to the variation in the speakers. Al-tanawul means taking hold, so the meaning is: he reached him and stabbed him with the spear, as if he had seized him; then "inthana lahu" means he stabbed him again, so he fell prostrate. He made it so for his hands and his mouth, because they are what first meet the earth when he falls upon his face. The lam here has the meaning of 'ala, as the grammarians have stated, though al-Nahhas denied it. Dalafa dalfan, like ta'iba ta'aban, means he advanced quickly and shortened his steps. Jaybu qamisihi is a metaphor for his chest, because if the collar of the shirt is torn by the spear, the chest has been torn.)

I say: its meaning is that He made their chins and faces for the falling and singled them out for it, because the lam denotes exclusivity (ikhtisas).

If you ask: why did He repeat "yakhurrun lil-adhqan" (they fall upon their chins)? I answer: because the two states differ. They fall while prostrating, and they fall while weeping.

Say: "Believe in it or do not believe." This is a command to turn away from them, to disregard them and to hold their affairs in contempt, and to pay no heed to them, to their faith, or to their refusal to accept it. Even if they do not enter into faith or accept the Qur'an, they are people of ignorance and polytheism. Yet those better and more excellent than them, namely the scholars who have read the scriptures and know what revelation (wahy) and the sacred laws (shara'i') are, have already believed in it and affirmed it. For them it has been established that he is the Arab Prophet promised in their scriptures. So when it is recited to them, they fall down prostrate, glorifying God in reverence for His command and for the fulfilment of what He promised in the revealed books, and of the good news of the sending of Muhammad ﷺ and the descent of the Qur'an upon him. This is what is meant by the promise in His words: ﴿Indeed the promise of our Lord is surely fulfilled.﴾ ...... ﴿And it increases them in humility﴾, that is, the Qur'an increases them in softness of heart and moistness of eye.

If you ask: what is the reason given by ﴿Indeed those who were given knowledge before it﴾? I answer: it may be a justification for His words "Believe in it or do not believe," and it may be a justification for "Say," by way of consolation for the Messenger of God ﷺ and to comfort his heart, as if it were said: "Console yourself regarding the faith of the ignorant with the faith of the scholars." On the first reading, the meaning is: "If you do not believe in it, then one better than you has believed in it."

If you ask: what is the meaning of falling down upon the chin (al-kharur lil-dhaqan)? I answer: it means falling onto the face. The chin (dhaqan), which is the meeting point of the two jaws, is mentioned because the one who prostrates first meets the earth with his chin. 

If you ask: the preposition of elevation (harf al-isti'la') is clear in meaning when you say "kharra 'ala wajhihi" (he fell upon his face) and "'ala dhaqanihi" (upon his chin), so what is the meaning of the lam in "kharra lidhaqanihi" and "li-wajhihi" (fell for/onto his chin and his face)? He said:

*So he fell prone, for both his hands and his mouth*

*At the Day of al-Kilab our spears had removed (him) ...
Sharahbil, when he swore an oath, a swearing one:*

*"He will surely snatch our spears," so he removed him,
Abu Hanash, from the back of a long, hard-hoofed mare.*

*He reached him with the spear, then turned back to him,
So he fell prone, for both his hands and his mouth.*

(This is attributed to Jabir al-Tha'labi. It is also said that the third line belongs to Shurayh al-'Absi, and it is also said to Zuhayr. Al-Kilab, with a dammah, is the name of the place of the battle. Ali means he swore. Al-shanqa' means a long mare, and al-saldam, with a kasra on the unpointed letters, means strong. It is also narrated as "thumma ith'na lahu," and the original is "inthana," where the nun was assimilated after being changed to a thaa'. If it were recited as "thumma a'tani" (from ataani, "came to me") and "tamahhala" (he delayed), it would be permissible. It is narrated as "dalafat lahu bil-rumh min tahti bazzihi" (I advanced to him with the spear from beneath his armour), and as "shaqqafat lahu bil-rumh jaybu qamisihi" (I pierced for him with the spear the collar of his shirt). The variation in the narrations is likely due to the variation in the speakers. Al-tanawul means taking hold, so the meaning is: he reached him and stabbed him with the spear, as if he had seized him; then "inthana lahu" means he stabbed him again, so he fell prostrate. He made it so for his hands and his mouth, because they are what first meet the earth when he falls upon his face. The lam here has the meaning of 'ala, as the grammarians have stated, though al-Nahhas denied it. Dalafa dalfan, like ta'iba ta'aban, means he advanced quickly and shortened his steps. Jaybu qamisihi is a metaphor for his chest, because if the collar of the shirt is torn by the spear, the chest has been torn.)

I say: its meaning is that He made their chins and faces for the falling and singled them out for it, because the lam denotes exclusivity (ikhtisas).

If you ask: why did He repeat "yakhurrun lil-adhqan" (they fall upon their chins)? I answer: because the two states differ. They fall while prostrating, and they fall while weeping.

On the authority of Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: Abu Jahl heard the Prophet (ﷺ) saying, "O Allah, O Most Merciful," and said, "He forbids us to worship two gods, yet he calls upon another god." It was also said that the People of the Book said, "You mention the Most Merciful a great deal, and Allah has mentioned this name often in the Torah," so this verse was revealed. Here, *al-du'a'* (calling upon) means naming, not calling out. It takes two objects. You say, "I named him Zayd" (*da'awtuhu Zaydan*), and then one object may be dropped when it is not needed, so you say, "I named Zayd" (*da'awtu Zaydan*).

﴿Allah﴾ and ﴿the Most Merciful﴾ refer to the names themselves, not to the one named. The *aw* (or) here is for choice. So the meaning of ﴿Call upon Allah or call upon the Most Merciful﴾ is: name Him by this name or by that name, and mention Him by either one. The *tanwin* (nunation, the "n" sound added to the end of a noun) on *ayyan* replaces the genitive noun that was added to it. The *ma* after *ayyan* is a *sila* (an added particle) that intensifies the vagueness already in *ayy*. The meaning is: whichever of these two names you name and mention, ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾. The pronoun in *falahu* does not refer to either of the two names mentioned. It refers to what they name, which is His Essence, because naming applies to the Essence and not to the name itself. The meaning is: whichever you call upon, it is good. The phrase ﴿to Him belong the most beautiful names﴾ is put in its place, because when all His names are good, these two names are good too, as they are among them. The meaning of their being the most beautiful names is that each one independently carries the meanings of praise, holiness and glory.

﴿Your prayer﴾ is read with the word for prayer (*salat*) and an omitted noun is understood, because there is no ambiguity. Loudness (*jahr*) and quietness (*mukhafatah*) are two qualities that alternate on the voice and nothing else, while prayer consists of actions and remembrance. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to raise his voice when reciting. When the polytheists heard it, they spoke idly and reviled, so he was commanded to lower his voice. The meaning is: do not be so loud that the polytheists hear you, and do not be so quiet that those behind you cannot hear you. ﴿Seek a middle way between them﴾ means a moderate path between loudness and quietness.

It is narrated that Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) used to recite quietly in his prayer and would say, "I am whispering to my Lord, and He knows my need." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) used to raise his voice and would say, "I drive away the devil and wake the drowsy." So the Prophet (ﷺ) told Abu Bakr to raise his voice a little, and told Umar to lower his voice a little. [[Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban and al-Hakim narrated it from the transmission of Yahya ibn Ishaq al-Sulayhini, from Hammad, from Thabit, from Abdullah ibn Rabah, from Abu Qatada, with the same meaning. It does not contain the phrase "He knows my need," and in it each of them spoke when the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him about it. Al-Tirmidhi said: most people narrated it without mentioning Abu Qatada. Ibn Abi Hatim said, quoting his father: the version containing Yahya ibn Ishaq is the wording, but the correct version is mursal (with a missing companion in the chain). There is a similar report from Ali, recorded by al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab. From Abu Hurayra, Abu Dawud recorded it through Muhammad ibn Umar. From Abu Salama, from him, in abridged form. al-Tabari recorded it through Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "I was told that Abu Bakr..." and mentioned it, and in it: "I am whispering to my Lord, and He knows my need."]] a little.

It was also said that the meaning is: do not raise your voice in all of your prayer, nor lower it in all of it, but seek a middle way between by loudly reciting at night prayers and quietly reciting at day prayers. It was also said that *bi-salatika* means *bi-du'a'ika* (in your supplication).

Some scholars held that the verse was abrogated by Allah's words ﴿Call upon your Lord humbly and secretly﴾. *Ibtigha' al-sabil* (seeking the way) is an image of aiming at the moderate course in recitation.

﴿Nor has He any ally out of weakness﴾ means: any helper who protects Him from humiliation, and any one who prevents it for Him. This is because of His might, or because He does not take an ally out of need of anyone, to repel humiliation through that alliance.

فإن قلت: كيف لاق وصفه بنفي الولد والشريك والذل بكلمة التحميد [[قال محمود: «إن قلت: كيف لاق وصفه بنفي الولد والشريك ... الخ» قال أحمد: وقد لاحظ الزمخشري هاهنا ما أغفله عند قوله تعالى الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ الَّذِي خَلَقَ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضَ وَجَعَلَ الظُّلُماتِ وَالنُّورَ ثُمَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا بِرَبِّهِمْ يَعْدِلُونَ وقد رددت هذا الوجه فيما تقدم، بأن هذه الجملة لا يليق اقترانها بكلمة التحميد ولا تناسبها، فإنك لو قلت ابتداء: الحمد لله الذي الذين كفروا به يعدلون، لم يكن مناسبا، والله أعلم.]] ؟ قلت: لأنّ من هذا وصفه هو الذي يقدر على إيلاء كل نعمة، فهو الذي يستحق جنس الحمد، وكان النبي ﷺ إذا أفصح الغلام من بنى عبد المطلب علمه هذه الآية [[أخرجه ابن أبى شيبة وعبد الرزاق. قالا أخبرنا ابن عيينة عن عبد الكريم عن عمرو بن شعيب عن أبيه عن جده.]] .

If you say: how does it fit that His description by the negation of offspring, partner, and humiliation is followed by the word of praise [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say: how does it fit his description by the negation of offspring and partner... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Here al-Zamakhshari noticed what he overlooked at the words of the Exalted, "Praise belongs to Allah, who created the heavens and the earth and made the darknesses and the light; then those who disbelieve in their Lord ascribe equals to Him" (6:1). I have already rejected this view earlier, on the ground that this sentence does not fit being joined to the word of praise nor suit it, for if you said at the outset, "Praise belongs to Allah, those who disbelieve in Him ascribe equals to Him," it would not be appropriate. And Allah knows best.]]? I say: because the one who has this description is the one who is able to bestow every blessing, so He alone deserves the whole category of praise. The Prophet ﷺ used to teach this verse to the boy of the family of ʿAbd al-Muttalib when he became articulate [[Narrated by Ibn Abi Shaybah and ʿAbd al-Razzaq. Both said: Ibn ʿUyaynah informed us, from ʿAbd al-Karim, from ʿAmr ibn Shuʿayb, from his father, from his grandfather.]].

From the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "Whoever recites Surat Bani Isra'il and his heart softens at the mention of the two parents, he will have a qintar in Paradise, and the qintar is a thousand uqiyyah and two hundred uqiyyah." May Allah grant us, by His abundant bounty and great kindness.
